You’re reading the Goings On newsletter, a guide to what we’re watching, listening to, and doing this week.
Sign up to receive it in your inbox.
When it comes to horror,
I’m a wimp. But, as a theatre critic, I’m fascinated by what catches on with audiences, and this season the genre is, unusually, front and center. The flagship production is Broadway’s
“
Paranormal Activity
”
(at the August Wilson, through Feb. 28), whose popularity recently prompted an eight-week extension of its run. Cunningly adapted by Levi Holloway from the hit movie franchise, the play follows Lou and James, a young couple who have moved to London from Chicago, hoping that the change will improve Lou’s mental health. Spoiler alert: it doesn’t.
Off Broadway, Danny Robins’s
“
2:22: A Ghost Story
”
(Lucille Lortel; through Jan. 17) also features a couple beset by troubles in their new home; the wife’s claim of a nightly haunting is put to the test when dinner guests stay up with them to witness it. Jamie Armitage’s
“
A Ghost in Your Ear
”
(Minetta Lane; through Dec. 12) equips audiences with headphones at the top of the show, literally plugging them into what happens onstage: an audiobook-recording session in which the story of a sadistic father seeps into the sound booth.
Illustration by Sam Kalda
If that’s not immersive enough, try Candle House Collective’s
“
claws
,”
by Evan Neiden, who specializes in remotely staged shows. In this one, you, the sole audience member, receive a phone call from a teen-ager begging for help, and it’s up to you to advise him. Still insufficiently realistic? Consider a
ghost tour of Merchant’s House
,
a residence turned museum where supernatural phenomena have been reported since the death of its last occupant, in 1933. When the building closed to the public during
COVID
, researchers investigated. Now one of them leads a 9:30
P.M.
tour, in which he shares findings that suggest—wait for it—paranormal activity.—
Dan Stahl
About Town
Alternative R. & B.
The singer-songwriter
Yebba
spent much of her initial breakout in mourning. A soloist in the classic soul and gospel traditions, she possesses a commanding and hypnotic voice that feels unignorable. But just as a performance of her original song “My Mind” was going viral, in 2016, her mother died. The elegant, sumptuous 2021 début she released in the aftermath, “Dawn,” dealt in processing that loss, rather than developing her personal style. This March, Yebba returned with the album “Jean,” and with a new directive: more reined-in, inward-looking music that is just as vulnerable yet focussed less on the power of her voice than on its character.—
Sheldon Pearce (
Brooklyn Paramount
; Nov. 2-3.)
Dance
About a decade ago,
Oona Doherty
, an Irish choreographer of rare and risk-taking honesty, made a name for herself with danced portraits of Belfast lads. Reacting to sudden fame, she swerved in other directions, but she has since swerved back with “Specky Clark.” A dance with dialogue, fuelled by the punkish sound of the Irish folk band Lankum, it takes the story of her great-great-grandfather working in an abattoir as a child and pushes it into Lynchian fantasy horror. On Samhain, the Gaelic festival during which boundaries between the living and the dead blur, he follows a pig into the spirit world. “Specky Clark” comes to the
Irish Arts Center
in time for Halloween.—
Brian Seibert (Oct. 25-Nov. 15.
)
Dance
Herman Cornejo in “Le Spectre de la Rose.”Photograph by Marty Sohl
American Ballet Theatre’s
fall season
is short and sweet, with three mixed bills plus a gala (Oct. 29). The latter includes both Frederick Ashton’s poetic male solo “Dance of the Blessed Spirits”—danced by the equally poetic Daniel Camargo—and Michel Fokine’s rococo “Le Spectre de la Rose.” In one program, Ashton’s undeniably magical “The Dream” (based on Shakespeare) will be performed alongside a new sextet, “Trio Élégiaque,” produced by a young dancer in the company, Brady Farrar. Another program is anchored by Natalia Makarova’s suite from the nineteenth-century Spanish-themed ballet “Paquita,” a tour de force of classical dance. And yet another offers a glimpse of Kyle Abraham’s stylish ensemble work “Mercurial Son,” in which the men of the company, in particular, have a chance to shine.—
Marina Harss (David H. Koch; Oct. 21-31.)
Off Broadway
“
The Curious Case of Benjamin Button
”
is a stunner—a gorgeously performed, gloriously staged, philosophically perverse fairy-tale musical that left me swooning. You may know the premise even if you haven’t read F. Scott Fitzgerald’s short story: a baby is born as an elderly man and ages backward; along the way, he struggles, has worldly adventures, and falls in love. Andrew Durand, with his handsome crab-apple features, makes a perfectly quizzical Benjamin; Kelsee Kimmel is stirring as his true love, who shares his age just once. The harmony-singing, instrument-playing ensemble is terrific, and the show’s strong score, by Darren Clark and Jethro Compton (who also wrote the book and directed), has a touch of “Hamilton” and a streak of “Come from Away.” Everything clicks: even the moon, swinging from a green net above the clever nautical set, stole the show.—
Emily Nussbaum (Public Theatre; through Dec. 6.)
Art
“The Shape of the Rock That’s Hurling Towards the Sea,” from 2022.
Art work by Celeste Dupuy-Spencer / Courtesy the Estate of Celeste Dupuy-Spencer / Jeffrey Deitch; Photograph by Joshua White / JW Pictures
A terrible weight hangs over “Burning in the Eyes of the Maker,” an exhibition of recent paintings by
Celeste Dupuy-Spencer.
The heaviness comes from the fact that the artist died in April, at age forty-six, but it’s also embedded in the paintings on view—in the bursts of fire and swirling floods that mark them. Dupuy-Spencer had a reputation for clear-eyed renderings of both the tenderness and the brutality of our world; here, darker forces prevail. Mythical beings hover over apocalyptic scenes crowded with tiny, ghostly figures, which seem to emerge from the paint. The monumental four-panel piece “The Shape of the Rock That’s Hurling Towards the Sea” (2022) is a parable in which only the rich seem to survive. But there’s one saving grace: the yellows, oranges, and reds of Dupuy-Spencer’s fires are achingly beautiful.—
Jillian Steinhauer (
Jeffrey Deitch
; through Oct. 31.)
Movies
The historical drama
“Fatherland,”
written and directed by Paweł Pawlikowski, zeroes in on an intriguing literary byway: the elderly, Nobel Prize-winning German novelist Thomas Mann’s trip to Germany in 1949, sixteen years after his self-exile upon Hitler taking power. The tale is energized by the thoughtful performances of Hanns Zischler, as Mann, and Sandra Hüller, as the author’s daughter Erika, who accompanies him while reviving conflicts from her own past. But the story, set amid Cold War tensions, and involving Mann’s vain belief in the importance of his visit to reconciling East and West, along with his nostalgic dream of a politics-free realm of art, is told with restrained images and a terse script that leave little room for dramatic complexity.—
Richard Brody (In limited release.)
Pick Three
Michael Schulman on downtown entertainers making grand returns.
1.
The sui-generis musical
“Hedwig and the Angry Inch”
originated as a gender-flouting, genre-busting phenomenon at the Jane Street Theatre, in 1998, performed by John Cameron Mitchell as the titular bewigged East German rocker. Mitchell wrote, directed, and starred in a movie version in 2001. (The songs are by Stephen Trask.) To celebrate the film’s twenty-fifth anniversary, Mitchell is touring the country with 4K screenings, followed by Q. & A.s and acoustic performances. The tour
hits the Beacon Theatre
on Nov. 16. Wigs welcome.
2.
The dearly departed Hulu sitcom “Difficult People” ran 2015-17, starring the comedians Julie Klausner (its creator) and Billy Eichner as snarky show-biz aspirants. The series was thick with pop-culture barbs, including ahead-of-the-curve digs at Kevin Spacey. Klausner and Alex Scordelis wrote an unproduced screenplay,
“Difficult People: The Movie,”
which she and other members of the original cast—including Eichner, Andrea Martin, James Urbaniak, and Gabourey Sidibe—will
read at The Town Hall
on Nov. 3, along with such special guests as Paul Walter Hauser, Cecily Strong, and Michael Urie.
Murray Hill.
Photograph by Gustavo Soriano
3.
The drag king Murray Hill has the look of a mustachioed Atlantic City lounge lizard and the shticky comic delivery of Don Rickles. In his moving new memoir,
“
Showbiz! My Life as a Middle-Aged Man
,”
Hill recounts his abusive childhood; his self-acceptance as a trans man; his breakout in New York’s downtown cabaret scene in the nineteen-nineties and then the burlesque revival of the two-thousands; the fire that destroyed his apartment on his fiftieth birthday; and his role as the bon vivant Fred Rococo on the HBO series “Somebody Somewhere.”

epub_5.text:
By
Hanif Abdurraqib
There is a moment I often recall that defines, for me, the ambition and affection that live in equal measure within the work of Andre D. Wagner. We were sitting together in a car, waiting at a stoplight, somewhere in one of the Carolinas, in 2019. A publication had come up with the idea of pairing a writer and a photographer for a week to explore a region of the country, then use whatever was gathered, between them, to tell a story. Wagner and I had never met before doing this assignment together. We’d done fairly well taking turns at the wheel, but on this particular day he had assumed most of the driving duties, a fact I must admit because it makes the moment in question more spectacular.
In the few seconds before the light changed, a group of young Black boys rode up alongside us on motorbikes. They sat piled two per bike, some with their shirts off, delighting in the gentle warmth of autumn on the horizon. Wagner, with one hand on the wheel, getting ready to drive off when the light turned green, aimed his camera toward the kids. And they, previously indifferent to our presence, became even more lively for the camera, throwing their hands up, smiling wide. It was a split second. It felt slow only because the camera existed within it, a vessel that freezes time but which, when in action, can also slow time.
I love the image that resulted from that interaction. I remember talking to Wagner about it, and him sharing something with me that I’ve thought about ever since: the idea that Black people are often photo-ready. Photo-eager. We’ve already got fly, we already believe ourselves to be fly: why
shouldn’t
someone want to take our photo? The boy holds on to the bare shoulders of the slightly larger boy on the front of a bike before it peels off. Why
wouldn’t
someone want to take their photo? The person listening to music through headphones and dancing in a universe made by and for them and no one else. The person crossing the street carrying shopping bags, wearing sunglasses, a bandanna, and a shirt with the words “
BLACK JOY
” blazoned across the front. When you point a camera at a Black person on the street, Wagner told me, the response, in so many cases, is one of embrace—of wanting to become a part of the archive, the archive of what the foolish might call the mundane, but we know better.
Wagner is exceptional at capturing tenderness. Looking through his photos, I feel aware that tenderness is not something you extract from others; it’s not something that operates as an exchange. People have to offer it to you. The photographs of his that I’m most deeply moved by show moments of profound, quiet interpersonal intimacy, the kind of interpersonal intimacy that you might take for granted if you are sharing it with someone you feel certain might love you forever. My favorite example shows a couple standing in front of a MetroCard machine in New York City. The photo was taken in 2020, and it seems like the world is shocked into a kind of stillness. The face of one subject is somewhat obscured, turned away from the camera. The other person, her eyes narrowed, leans her face into the towering, curly Afro of her partner, who rests a hand on her rear end. It looks as if she is slipping into a dream. I love this photo of the couple for their expression of affection toward each other, and I love how that affection presses up against the world—the stillness of the world, the distance of the world. Maybe they’re going places. Maybe they aren’t. Maybe the sidewalk has become theirs, their own universe, which no one else can access.
I love Wagner’s photos of these tender human interactions, because they provide more questions than answers, which is a gift of the still image. You don’t need to know anyone pictured; you don’t need to know their stories. You can project whatever you imagine onto what you’re being offered. This, I think, is what Gordon Parks meant when he said that the content of a photograph should be determined by “the heart, not the eye.” The eye sees an image; the heart sees a story.
Perhaps there’s another truth tucked under the truth of camera-readiness that Wagner shared with me that day: we always look kind of cool, our angles are deeply known to us, and we walk into the world waiting for someone to illuminate them. We don’t have to be told that we are fly, but it doesn’t hurt to get some confirmation, by way of a camera pointing in our direction. In another favorite photo, a young Black sailor blows smoke into the air. He is wearing the attire of someone who has just finished naval basic training—a white sailor’s suit. He’s looking straight ahead, a slight smirk on his face, the smoke largely obscuring the faces of his peers next to him. The smoke is as much a character in the photo as the man himself. It’s like a magic trick, the smoke brings the subject further into focus. And it’s such a nonchalant gesture, something you might see every day on city blocks. But you’ve not seen this specific person, in this specific corner of the world. You maybe haven’t seen someone who knows he is fly, even fresh out of a military program that strives to make you shed that which makes you unique. It is beautiful, this photo. It captures all of our flyness, in opposition to a world that tries to dull its shine.
This is drawn from “
Andre D. Wagner: New City, Old Blues
.”

Comment
The Republicans’ Remarkably Bad Midterm Campaigns
Things were going poorly even before Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign ran the most offensive ad of the year.
By
Benjamin Wallace-Wells
Photo illustration by Cristiana Couceiro; Source photograph from Getty
The midterm campaigns have been going badly enough for the Republicans that they have inspired in White House principals some rare candor. “You don’t turn the Titanic around overnight,” Vice-President J. D. Vance said on the trail earlier this year, in Toledo. He was speaking about the economy, but the same might be said now about the second term of Donald Trump, or, perhaps, about Vance’s own political prospects; on Tuesday, the President said that it was “very early” to endorse him as his preferred successor. Later that day, Trump was in North Carolina, a state that he won in the 2024 Presidential election, but where his handpicked Senate candidate, Michael Whatley, is trailing by so much that the G.O.P. has essentially stopped putting money into the race. On Wednesday afternoon, at a rally in Greenville, Trump said of Whatley’s Democratic opponent, Roy Cooper, “He’s going to become your senator. And it’s crazy.”
It is at least a little crazy how sharply politics have turned on the Republicans. Last week, prediction markets favored Democrats to win Senate races not just in North Carolina but in Ohio, which Trump won in 2024 by more than ten points, and in Alaska and Texas, each of which he won by thirteen points. Democrats are still underdogs in Kansas, which their party last represented in the Senate in 1939, and in Iowa, but they are drawing close. By Wednesday, when a headline on
Axios
read “Senate Republicans Fear Mississippi Is in Play,” things had started to feel a little surreal. The Republican predicament was summed up by an apparent A.I. prompt, mistakenly published on the website of Eric Pratt, a nominee for Congress in Minnesota: “The President is not popular, so all messaging should be focused on local politics and needs.”
On this point, most Republican candidates have seemed on message. A
Times
analysis found that more than ninety-nine per cent of G.O.P. ad spending is now going to spots that do not mention Trump. But even that strategy is backfiring. The campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy, who is running for governor in Vance’s home state of Ohio, paid for an ad in which the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, a doctor and the former director of the state health department, denounced her. The ad neglected to note that Acton had been removed from her mother’s care when she was twelve, after her stepfather was indicted on a charge of raping her. Several prominent Ohio Republicans, including Senator Jon Husted, who is up for reëlection, disavowed the ad; Vance dismissed their objections as “whining,” while Trump said that the ad had hit “pay dirt.”
A similar fissure has appeared in some Senate debates. In Minnesota, the G.O.P. nominee, Michele Tafoya, answered the opening question by referring to “a number of areas where I’m going to disagree with the President.” (She also called the killings in her state of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, by federal law-enforcement agents, “devastating.”) In Michigan, the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers, said, a bit testily, that the President’s high-profile tariffs on goods from Canada “were not well thought through.” In Maine, the longtime Republican incumbent, Susan Collins, bragged that she had voted against Trump more often than she’d voted against Joe Biden. Even the Alaska senator Dan Sullivan, who has been a reliable party-line vote for Trump, said that sometimes he will “forcefully oppose” things “in private.”
One policy choice that Republicans have started to oppose in public is, in retrospect, the pivotal decision of the midterms, and likely of Trump’s second term: the war in Iran. Trump’s approval ratings have never been especially high this term, but they began to drop below forty per cent around late March, a month after the war started, and have steadily declined since then. The elections analyst Nate Silver noted last week that Trump’s ratings were nearly as bad as George W. Bush’s were in his second term. The war has, as predicted, driven up both energy prices and inflation—a situation that has made it much harder for Republican candidates to convincingly claim that their businessman President is doing anything about affordability. It has also forced those same candidates to try to defend a war that few believe in. (
The Atlantic
reported that even Donald Trump, Jr., has taken issue with his father over it—in private.) During an Iowa Senate debate, the moderators displayed images of two soldiers, native Iowans, killed in action in the Middle East.
In Iowa and in other Midwestern states, the price of diesel, which has risen more sharply than other fuel prices, has become a potent political issue. In response, Trump waived U.S. policy and announced a deal in October with President Vladimir Putin to purchase hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel. A week later, Trump suspended a sanctions package on Russia—named for Lindsey Graham, the late Republican senator from South Carolina, who made the war in Ukraine his signature fight—which the Senate had passed and the President himself signed in September. Meanwhile, Elon Musk, who has spent more than four hundred million dollars on Republican campaigns this election cycle, slowed Ukraine’s access to his Starshield satellite network, leaving that country more vulnerable to Russian attacks. For some Republicans, this was too much. On Wednesday, Ashley Hinson, a politically savvy congresswoman who is the Senate nominee in Iowa, said before a joint rally with the President that she would tell Trump to his face that the deal with Putin was “a bad idea.”
It is also a betrayal. On Wednesday night, Trump campaigned in South Carolina with Darline Graham, who was appointed, at Trump’s behest, to finish her brother’s Senate term, and who championed the Russian-sanctions bill. She has often said on the campaign trail, “I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia.” But she is in a surprisingly competitive race in a deep-red state, and she needs Trump’s help to win there, even if it is largely his fault that she might lose. At the rally, she watched as the President casually told a story of calling Putin and asking for a favor, as if to make a show of how responsive the Russian leader is to him. War is horrific, but clarifying. It has exposed Trump, to at least a segment of the public that has long stood with him, as someone who stands not with them but with the oligarchs. And it has shown politicians like Graham and Hinson exactly the terms of the deal they have made. ♦

Bad News, Good News Dept.
For Bob Iger, That’s the Way It Is
The former Ithaca weatherman became Disney’s C.E.O. Now he’s just like everyone else—retired and co-owning the Los Angeles Lakers with Josh Kushner, by way of Karlie Kloss.
By
Ben McGrath
Illustration by João Fazenda
You’re reading
The Talk of the Town
: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
Bob Iger took a seat on a balcony outside the Perelman Performing Arts Center, in lower Manhattan, the other day and ran a hand gently over his right knee. He was unshaven and dressed casually, in a black V-neck over a white T-shirt, black pants, and black-and-white Nikes. “It’s my second knee, and it’s a slog,” he said, alluding to recent surgery. “Not to complain, but it’s kind of barbaric—they literally saw the top of your tibia off, and the bottom of your femur. They replace what was there with metal. And they tell you to walk that day, and they send you home. So there’s a lot of pain management.”
Iger, who stepped down as the C.E.O. of
Disney
in March, votes and pays taxes in California, but he has long maintained an apartment in New York. “I have four adult kids,” he said. “They all live here—and five grandchildren.” He had spent the previous day at the apartment, watching football with two twentysomething sons and noticed, with a veteran media man’s weary resignation, that their attention was “somewhat diverted,” as he put it, by the rectangles in their hands.
Iger was soon to receive an Icon of Culture award from
PAC
, and that achievement, plus a looming acquisition of the
Los Angeles Lakers
, gave him occasion to reflect on what he viewed as an unlikely career. It began in 1973, after he graduated from Ithaca College with dreams of becoming an anchorman. “Who wouldn’t want to be Walter Cronkite?” he said, recalling his habit, as a preteen on Long Island, of devouring the
Times
before school. “Air-raid drills, the Kennedy era and assassination, the birth of the Beatles, and the Vietnam War and free love. It was a very, very rich time.”
He started, instead, as an Ithaca weatherman. “It was a great experience, because it taught me how to give people bad news,” he said. A roof over the balcony shielded him from gusting wind that left commuters turtling their necks into sweaters. “If we were in Ithaca, it would probably be a little bit colder and a little bit wetter.”
Ithaca was on a lot of minds for a different kind of bad news, involving an
alleged gang rape at Cornell
that had become another proxy battle in the culture wars. “We don’t have to talk about it,” Iger said. He meant this not just as an evasion but symbolically. Too many opinions. He had turned out to be better at delivering bad news off camera than on: a quiet consensus builder with a ruthless streak. Ten years ago, like not a few executives of his generation, he thought about going into politics, as a pragmatic centrist. “I sensed that there was a disillusionment with the state of political affairs and that people were looking for more outsiders to get involved,” he said. Then, having missed his Trump moment, he watched as politics invaded the theme parks, the airwaves, and the boardroom alike, with everyone spouting off. “I spent a lot of time not just reminding people but exhorting people to focus on what our No. 1 goal was, which was to entertain,” he said. “Walt Disney created Disneyland in part to enable people to put their daily frets aside and just cocoon themselves in a happy experience.” He added, “The company had to pull people back and remind them that, in a way, you give up your private-citizen status.”
He brought up a recent
Times
story about political polarization across the globe and contrasted it with what he’d seen during the
World Cup
—foreigners happily drinking their way through American cities. “There’s something about sports that’s a uniting factor,” he said. This brought him to the Lakers deal, worth a reported $12.5 billion, with Josh Kushner as a business partner. “My relationship with Josh began with his then girlfriend, Karlie Kloss, asking me if I could spend some time with her boyfriend,” Iger marvelled. Kloss, a supermodel, was friends with Iger’s wife, Willow Bay, a former model and the dean of the journalism school at U.S.C. Kushner showed up to their first meeting with a list of annotated questions—“I can’t remember if there were Post-it notes, or whatever”—about leadership techniques.
Iger’s hand returned to his knee. Sitting left it behaving like a “rusty gate,” he said. He stood and glanced toward the reflecting pools in the footprint of the old Twin Towers and recalled that his best friend from Ithaca, Jay Fischler, had become a battalion chief in the New York City Fire Department. “I spent seventy-two hours listening to his answering machine, hoping that he’d pick up,” he said, thinking back to 9/11, but in the middle of the crisis there was no one to deliver the good news that Fischler was alive and well. ♦

The Pictures
A Pickpocket’s Guide to New York
Preparing to play a petty thief in a new movie, John Turturro learned the moves—“reefing the kick” among them—from Apollo Robbins, and observed how much stealing has in common with acting.
By
Michael Schulman
Illustration by João Fazenda
John Turturro slipped into Madison Square Park and greeted a man sitting inconspicuously in a black coat and a fedora. In the new film “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” directed by Noah Segan, Turturro plays an old-school thief named Harry—a holdover from the era of subway graffiti, lost in the brave new world of cryptocurrency—who provokes the Mob when he unwittingly lifts a flash drive from the wrong guy. The man on the park bench was his pickpocketing consultant, Apollo Robbins. Known as “the gentleman thief,” Robbins spent years as a Vegas entertainer, relieving willing spectators of their wallets, watches, and rings (and then giving them back).
As this magazine reported, in 2012
, he once cleaned out the pockets of
Jimmy Carter
’s Secret Service detail: itinerary, badges, keys to the motorcade.
“His hands—he’s like a concert pianist!” Turturro said. Robbins had tutored him at the movie’s production office, where they practiced techniques on a stunt guy and devised Harry’s steals. (“Like a fight choreographer,” Robbins said. “But I was a theft choreographer.”) They considered having Robbins act as a hand double, but Turturro wanted to bring off the grabs himself. Among other things, he had learned from Robbins that a pickpocket’s gait changes after a steal. “You just want to disappear,” Turturro said, demonstrating how to blend in with the crowd.
A woman approached Turturro to tell him that her son used to play basketball with his. After she left, Robbins revealed that he’d cased her: two bags, one slung around her back, the other under her arm. “So probably her valuables would be there,” he said. “Usually, you’d just cut the bag and drop the contents out.” He took a leather wallet from his coat. “They used to have a term called ‘peeking the poke,’ ” he went on. “ ‘Poke’ was another name for wallet, so peeking the poke was: Where is this going to be? If it’s in the inside pocket, that’s called ‘the pit,’ or ‘uptown.’ ”
“I’m going uptown!” Turturro said, relishing the lingo. The actor had never been pickpocketed himself, but when he worked as a bartender in the seventies he’d been robbed at knifepoint. The ethics of pickpocketing intrigued him; unlike mugging, it’s usually nonviolent and requires finesse. “There’s a balletic aspect to it,” he said. Turturro found pickpocketing a bit like acting, insofar as he is stealing from life to create a character. “You stitch it together,” he continued. “But you are a thief in the night sometimes.”
Robbins showed off a move called “reefing the kick”: using your fingers to walk an item up to the top of someone’s pocket from the outside. The resurgence of baggy jeans, he said, has been good for pickpockets. “There’s a fine line between fondling and pickpocketing,” he cautioned.
“Too bad that line’s not in the movie,” Turturro said. A young red-headed guy came up and introduced himself as Zane Roth, a sometime magician. “Can we rob you?” Turturro asked. Robbins had Roth hold out his wrist, and showed how he would pop off the strap of his watch. After a few minutes, he handed Roth his wallet, having filched it from his front pocket during the conversation. Impressive enough. Then Robbins asked for Turturro’s wallet, from which he produced Roth’s student I.D.
Growing up in Springfield, Missouri, Robbins had two older half brothers who stole for a living, before moving on to bigger crimes. He pulled off his first notable feat at age eleven, pocketing some cigarettes at a convenience store. The manager confronted him, and he slipped them into the man’s apron. (Robbins’s father, a preacher, later tried to exorcise him.) At fourteen, he discovered magic. “I started seeking mentors in both worlds”—crime and magic—“and created a hybrid out of those two,” he said.
Robbins has studied “theft culture” around the world. In China, pickpockets use chopsticks, and bystanders tend not to interfere. In Japan, subway riders cram together but spread out once they’re off the train. Technology is a mixed bag: people are distracted by their phones, making themselves easier marks, but increased surveillance means that pickpockets have to fool the cameras as well as their victims.
Thieves used to contact Robbins, but he’s less keyed-in now. “There are different criteria when you have a family,” he said. “How much time do I want to spend with criminal networks?” A few years ago, he gave up full-time performing and now runs a security company called Ludus Labs, using his insights into misdirection and deception to advise government contractors. He still pickpockets at client presentations—U.S. marshals, chiefs of police—to demonstrate blind spots in critical thinking. “The stealing is now a metaphor,” he said. “I’ve become a walking analogy.” ♦

Dept. of Dishes
Daniel Humm’s Home Décor
The Eleven Madison Park chef surveys his cozy new restaurant in the West Village with the artists who decked it out, Rashid Johnson and Francesco Clemente.
By
Emma Allen
Illustration by João Fazenda
You’re reading
The Talk of the Town
: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
If you’ve watched a Hallmark movie, you’ve likely encountered the
Robert Frost
line “Home is the place where, when you have to go there, they have to take you in.” Which is a nice idea, unless you misheard and “home” is actually the new, seven-thousand-square-foot West Village restaurant Humm, where it’ll be nearly impossible to get a reservation for the foreseeable future.
But Humm is a decidedly homey, nostalgic place, with garnet, sage, and ochre velvet seats and a central hearth, which was not yet lit when Daniel Humm, the chef known for his decades at the helm of
Eleven Madison Park
—the standard-bearer for lavish tasting menus—surveyed the space a few weeks before its opening.
Humm said he believed that all his restaurants were “soulful” but noted that “everything on this menu is very recognizable—the roast chicken here is my mom’s roast chicken. She would stuff it under the skin with a bread-crumb-lemon crust, or on Christmas she made it with foie gras and truffles.”
In strolled the artist
Francesco Clemente
. He’d spent months painting the dining room’s ceiling with stars, trains, and clocks. In the eighties, Clemente had decorated the walls of the Palladium, a Steve Rubell night club. “I remember what my attitude was then, and it’s the same now,” Clemente said. “To make something that would feel as if it was there before the space, like something that maybe had been covered up over time.”
Humm’s father was an architect. “He introduced me to this idea of a
Gesamtkunstwerk
,” Humm said. “That’s what I think a restaurant is—the way Richard Wagner composed his sets.” When Humm was ten, his parents took him to the Musée de l’Orangerie, in Paris, and he wept in front of Monet’s water lilies. “I just didn’t know—was I sad or was I happy?” he recalled.
The artist
Rashid Johnson
, who’d also made works for the restaurant, showed up and wished Humm a happy (belated) birthday. Humm said that another painter pal, Rita Ackermann, had cooked goulash for him on the big day. Johnson’s birthday, meanwhile, was coming up—on it, he’d be cooking for Humm and his wife. “I make chili,” Johnson said. “Or I do, like, a pork-chop dish. It’s not like Daniel’s judging my fucking cooking.”
Johnson gazed at one of his own paintings, which hangs in the dark-red lounge and features outlines of houses. “I was making these works that were about the way we interrogate ‘home’ from a very simplistic position but also from a very complicated one, and how you think about that duality around neighborhood, collective housing, how we think about shelters, how we imagine ourselves inhabiting these spaces,” he said.
The trio settled in to draw on sheets of paper with circles printed on them, which Humm uses to come up with dishes.
“Is this the size of the plates?” Johnson asked.
“No, this is the idea of the plate,” Humm responded.
“Radiator spirit, we implore you to turn on and heat our apartment to a reasonable temperature that’s not too, too hot. . . .”
Cartoon by Sarah Kempa
Johnson grabbed a pencil and divided his “plate” into thirds, which he labelled “V,” “M,” and “C” (vegetables, meat, and carbs).
“I’m glad you didn’t say ‘protein,’ ” Clemente said.
Humm outlined two cutlets. “So, this is, like, a chicken,” he explained.
“I see a salad,” Clemente said.
“Francesco is very lucky because Alba, his wife, is one of the best cooks on the planet,” Humm said, as he added yellow mushrooms to his composition. “For me, a dish is like a feeling, really. Of course, visually, we want to do something pleasing, but I don’t think of a plate like a painting.” (Counterpoint: the artist Paul McCarthy purportedly declared, upon eating Humm’s celery root cooked in a pig’s bladder, “Oh, my God, I feel like I’m eating a painting by Robert Ryman.”)
Clemente mused, “One paints for the dead and cooks for the living.”
“When you make art, you’re in this conversation with a lot of dead people,” Johnson agreed.
Humm mentioned a portrait of his wife that hangs in their dining room at home. He said, “Francesco painted it for my proposal to her.” Humm had bought an engagement ring and shown it to Clemente to incorporate into the work in progress. “Are you sure she’s going to say yes?” Clemente had asked. Humm proposed in the artist’s studio, in front of the finished painting.
The men completed their drawings. Clemente described his plate as “autobiographical—depressed, in a panic.” Johnson had obscured his original “V-M-C” with swirling rainbow lines. “I make these characters, I think of them as souls,” he said.
Humm asked Johnson how he liked the velvet chairs. “You know what you want in a chair when you’re at a restaurant?” Johnson replied. “Not to think about the chair that you’re sitting in. So the fact that I haven’t noticed it is a very fucking good sign.” ♦

The Boards
From the Battalion to Broadway
Alex Ekker served four years in the Marine Corps—then decided to be an actor. While sightseeing at the Empire State Building, he talks about his professional début in Aaron Sorkin’s “A Few Good Men.”
By
Sarah Larson
Illustration by João Fazenda
You’re reading
The Talk of the Town
: fun, fizzy dispatches from the city and beyond.
Like the gung-ho sailors of “On the Town,” the actor Alex Ekker, twenty-seven, is a military man new to New York City and game for sightseeing. Ekker, who has kind eyes, close-cropped hair, and excellent posture (How tall? “Six-two, but people say I’m six-four for some reason”), served in the U.S. Marine Corps for four years, and currently plays a marine in Aaron Sorkin’s “A Few Good Men” at Lincoln Center. On a recent day off, he cheerfully stuck to a plan to visit the Empire State Building, despite fog, wind, and a downpour; presumably, he’s endured worse. “There’s zero-per-cent visibility,” a gruff guard said at the entrance, with a hint of
What’s wrong with you idiots?
Ekker, in a zip-up jacket and khakis, proceeded through the building’s near-empty museum, enjoying its immersive marvels: twenties street scene; theatre of E.S.B. fare (he’d seen “Sleepless in Seattle,” “ ‘Superman,’ of course,” and “the Jack Black ‘King Kong’ ”); Kong room, with vibrating ape hands. The elevator simulated the skyscraper’s construction, complete with New York accents. “It’s an amusement-park ride,” Ekker said. “What is going on?”
On the eighty-sixth floor, he ventured toward the observation deck: “Ready to brave it?” Outside was blustery, loud, hail-like. “Whoa, yeah!” Ekker yelled, with military vigor. He gazed out at the fog. “It’s hard to see any of the lights,” he observed. “Oh, there’s some stuff! Whoo!” A few lights, possibly a river. Ekker laughed and headed back in: “Oh, my goodness gracious.”
Ekker was cast in Sorkin’s play this summer, having just graduated from acting school in North Carolina; his Broadway début is also his professional début. “A Few Good Men” (in movie form: Tom Cruise, Jack Nicholson, “You can’t handle the truth!”) centers on a court-martial of two marines and a possible coverup. In this production, featuring the Sorkin veteran Bradley Whitford, Ekker’s roles include regular M.P. (“Ten-hut”) and sergeant at arms (“Ten-
hut!
”). He also understudies two others. “I’m excited, if the day comes,” he said. “But I like my tribe now, and I get to wear the dress blues.”
An indoor gelato stand sold Empire State Building Hot Chocolate; Ekker got in line. “I never thought I wanted to be an actor,” he said. “I love stories. In the Marines, I met people from all around the world, listened to these incredible things. . . . I think we have a sheltered view here.” When his service ended, he decided to try acting. He said, “I wanted to express, in a way, what I wanted to do when I joined the Marine Corps”—to help people. “I didn’t know exactly how to fit in with everybody when I was younger, and I hated bullies. But I love people—or what people are capable of.”
Ekker, the son of two now retired Navy officers, grew up in Virginia Beach and Chesapeake. As a kid, he admired marines, who’d come to his school for Toys for Tots drives; his parents admired them, too. “I wanted to be a protector,” Ekker said. He enlisted at nineteen. Boot camp was humbling, he said, but later “you think, ‘Why was I such a wimp?’ ” He loved the marines’ unbreakable brotherhood (“You’re in the suck together, and the barriers fall away”) and learned about “what honor means for different people.” In “A Few Good Men,” he said, “everybody is fighting for what they think is right, a lot of them for a greater cause. How much has to be sacrificed in order for it to work? And maybe it’s the greater good, maybe not.” His E.S.B. Hot Chocolate was ready—and towering. “Whoa,” he said. “It’s mostly whipped cream!”
After the Marines, “going to an arts conservatory was a complete one-eighty,” he went on. From brotherhood “no matter what you say to the guy next to you” to “Oh, man, I have no idea what anybody’s talking about. I don’t know the next-generation celebrities. I don’t know why everybody’s singing and dancing.” But his acting cohort became a family, too.
Before leaving, he took one more spin around the observation deck. “I wonder what this looks like from the ground,” he said. He looked up, to a beautiful sight: the top of the Empire State Building, glowing like a lighthouse in the fog. And between it and him, an old, somewhat tattered friend. “The American flag!” Ekker said, taking a picture. “This is so awesome.” Afterward, on the sidewalk, a tourist approached. “Where is the Empire State Building?” he asked. Ekker lit up. “Just go around the corner and turn left,” he said. ♦
