Annals of Diplomacy
Charles Kushner and the MAGA Ambassador’s Playbook
Since taking up his post in Paris, Kushner has become known for lobbing provocations onto France’s domestic scene at sensitive moments. As he put it, “Nobody has the courage to say what I say.”
By
Lauren Collins
Kushner said, of blowing off the French government’s request for a meeting, “I’m not getting called to the principal at this stage in my life.”Illustration by Barry Blitt
In July, to fête America on its Semiquincentennial, Charles Kushner, the United States Ambassador to France and Monaco, hosted a lavish party at his official residence, the Hôtel de Pontalba, in Paris. Louis XV-style sofas, adorned with throw pillows in stars and stripes, dotted the villa’s enormous lawn. Servers circulated in cigarette-girl fashion, carrying wicker baskets loaded with little glass bowls of dorade ceviche, as French guests in military dress perused a spread of fajitas, pronouncing the dish with a hard “j.” (Per a placard, all the food was “kosher and prepared under rabbinical supervision.”) Like his boss back in Washington, Kushner had undertaken an ambitious makeover of his temporary home, funded largely by donations from French businesspeople. He planned to add A.C., and had fixed the building’s façade, which had been held together with steel mesh to keep concrete from falling on people’s heads. “Literally, we did power washing, and we had six foot of balustrades that came off,” Kushner told me later. “This is America’s home, and it was not dignified.”
During previous Fourth of July celebrations at the Embassy, guests had mingled freely, but now a V.I.P. section had been installed toward the front of the garden, cordoned off by red velvet ropes. The imposition of such a hierarchy seemed an odd choice for an event celebrating the birth of one democracy on the soil of another—more bridge-and-tunnel than all-men-are-created-equal or
liberté-égalité-fraternité
. But it was in keeping with the Kushner family’s predilection for conducting public service as a private affair, and with Kushner’s role as an exemplar of
MAGA
-style diplomacy in Donald Trump’s second term.
Since taking up his post, in the summer of 2025, Kushner has gained a reputation for lobbing provocations onto France’s domestic scene at sensitive moments. Just six weeks after arriving in the country, he published an open letter to President Emmanuel Macron in the
Wall Street Journal
, accusing him of allowing France to become a bastion of antisemitism. Ambassadors are ostensibly bound by Article 41 of the 1961 Vienna Convention, which forbids them to interfere in their host country’s internal affairs. In response to the open letter, the French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, took the unusual step of issuing Kushner a summons, an official demand that he appear for a meeting. Kushner ignored the request.
About six months later, in February of 2026, a far-right activist died of a brain injury after being beaten by members of a far-left group following a street brawl in Lyon. As with the assassination of Charlie Kirk, the event prompted an onslaught of uninformed commentary and partisan distortion. French authorities urged people to avoid politicizing the incident while an investigation was under way, but Kushner’s office did not oblige. “Violent left-wing extremism is on the rise,” the American Embassy pronounced on X. In an unprecedented back-to-back censure, Barrot convoked Kushner again. When Kushner flouted that summons, too, Barrot temporarily barred him from meeting with members of the French government, citing his “apparent misunderstanding of the basic expectations of an ambassador.”
Kushner may have belatedly learned his lesson. In early October, French high-school students, protesting poor learning conditions, blocked the entrances to their schools, setting off demonstrations that have spread across Europe. Trump saw a midterm-friendly angle in the mayhem, calling the French protests the result of “Islam” and “mass migration,” but Kushner rejected his boss’s assertion. He told me, “I would not make that broad generalization.” His French bodyguards had explained that their compatriots are “professional protesters,” he said. Even after October 17th, when a day of demonstrations ended with vandals attacking government buildings and looting thousands of shops, he declined to join the Administration in pointing fingers. “I can’t stop thinking about those small-business owners who lost everything—it’s heartbreaking,” he said, adding, “Our top priority is keeping Americans safe.”
In recent decades, under both Democratic and Republican Presidents, around seventy per cent of ambassadorships have been filled by career diplomats rather than by political appointees. By contrast, only about twenty per cent of the ambassadors whom Trump has tapped since his reëlection have any professional experience in diplomacy. His hundred and twenty-two appointees have included a restaurant mogul, a Broadway-musical producer, a former N.F.L. running back, and the President’s eldest son’s ex-fiancée. The last of these, Kimberly Guilfoyle, was night-clubbing and brokering energy deals from Athens until she was forced to resign, in mid-October, in response to allegations that she’d asked a G.O.P. donor to wire a hundred thousand dollars to pay off her American Express bill. The restaurant guy, Tilman Fertitta, is posted in Rome. Over the summer, in a video shared on Instagram in which he wandered around his four-hundred-and-fifty-million-dollar superyacht with a plastic cup in hand, he announced that he would be conducting a program of “coastal diplomacy” to honor America’s birthday by touring thirteen regions “to meet and celebrate with hundreds of Italians from local communities.” In other words, he was going on a cruise. Eric Rubin, a former U.S. Ambassador to Bulgaria, told me, “Every Administration has what we call ‘clunkers,’ but we’ve never had quite this number of flagrantly unqualified people.”
Even among this cohort, Kushner, a New Jersey real-estate developer who happens to be the father of Trump’s son-in-law Jared, stands out. He does not speak French. He has never lived abroad. He served time in federal prison for illegal campaign contributions, tax evasion, and witness tampering, and was later pardoned by Trump, in 2020. The last crime, a blackmail scheme that involved hiring a prostitute to seduce his sister’s husband, suggests a dubious approach to conflict management. By Kushner’s own admission, he lacks the “natural ingredients for diplomacy,” as he told the
Times
. Yet Trump saw fit to hand him one of the most coveted posts in American diplomacy, the seat once held by Thomas Jefferson and by Benjamin Franklin, stewarding the relationship with America’s oldest ally. (Kushner told me that the “family issue” had “probably zero” to do with his appointment.)
That Kushner even managed to secure agrément, whereby a state accepts a foreign ambassador’s nomination, was a little miracle of American hegemony. Peter Ricketts, a former British Ambassador to France, observed, “Coming from any other country, they’d probably have said, ‘No, thanks.’ ” Many American career diplomats were taken aback. “The guy’s a former convict, and a pretty seedy and salacious one, at that,” Lew Lukens, a former U.S. Ambassador to Senegal and Guinea-Bissau, told me. “I don’t know how anyone’s not shocked by the notion that he’s the best person to represent the United States in France.”
On America’s birthday, at least, Kushner’s mood was persuasively statesmanlike. Behind the velvet ropes, he appeared at a lectern, a white-haired Jared doppelgänger in a dark suit and a red power tie, and delivered a speech paying tribute to the long-standing symbiosis between France and America and the “blood mingled” on the battlefields of Yorktown and the beaches of Normandy.
The reason for this unusually Francophile display became surmisable when Kushner welcomed his guest of honor, his friend Bernard Arnault, the head of the luxury-goods conglomerate L.V.M.H. and a major sponsor of the evening. The invitation was both a Trumpist statement—Arnault, one of the richest men in the world, embodies what
Le Monde
has called “the inversion of the balance of power between politics and business”—and a mark of personal admiration. Kushner, minutes earlier so composed, bobbled his words and told Arnault that he was “beyond grateful” for his attendance, as the garden filled with the unmistakable scent of a man crush.
“That’s my off-site storage facility.”
Cartoon by Amy Hwang
As a treat for Arnault and his wife, Hélène, a concert pianist, the Kushners had arranged for a performance by Andrea Bocelli. The tenor emerged in an iridescent dinner jacket and blue-tinted sunglasses. The sky was darkening as Bocelli told the guests, “I think you know this song, if you want to sing along with me,” and launched into “Nessun dorma,” a Trump-rally staple.
When the show was over, I walked up to the V.I.P. area and tried to step behind one of the velvet ropes, but a man in a U.S.-military uniform rebuffed my approach. A fireworks display began, and guests filtered home while strains of Frank Sinatra’s “New York, New York” carried over the garden walls.
France became the new American nation’s ally in 1778, when Louis XVI signed the first treaty recognizing the United States’ sovereignty. Less than two decades later, the bond was tested by a scandal known as the XYZ Affair, in which France’s foreign minister, Talleyrand, demanded bribes from American envoys to Paris. More recently, the French and American governments have sparred over such issues as the Iraq War, N.S.A. spying, tariffs, the war in Ukraine, Greenland, and
NATO
funding. Kushner’s fraught relations, however, are notable for being a product largely of his own making. He has shown scant interest in his host country. Introducing himself to the French public in a social-media video, he said that he knew “a limited amount about France” but that he and his wife, Seryl, came often on her birthday, to “walk down the Champs-Élysées and just enjoy.” (This is kind of like saying that what you really like to do on your very regular visits to New York City is stroll around Times Square.) The sight of a packed café has been known to leave him wondering if Parisians ever go to work.
Kushner’s esteem for public servants has likewise tended to hover somewhere between condescension and outright disgust. He once vented to the trade publication
The Real Deal
about “stupid ethics watchdogs,” complaining, “All they want to do is assure that poor, not successful people go into government.” Kushner so far has participated little in the ceremony of the job, avoiding most receptions and ribbon cuttings. The French news channel TF1 once mistakenly referred to him as Jared. He prefers to go where he can make an impact, his advisers said, pointing to successes in bringing the N.F.L. to Paris, for its first-ever regular-season game in France; increasing French investment in the U.S.; and expanding opportunities for American businesses in France. Last spring, I was told that he hadn’t been doing many public events—it would be unseemly to be quaffing champagne in Paris as America dropped bombs on Iran. That didn’t stop Kushner from hosting a party to celebrate the release of “Melania,” the First Lady’s Amazon-backed documentary. Guests were invited to enjoy a “private screening in the presence of the film’s director, Mr. Brett Ratner,” who has been accused by multiple women of sexual misconduct. (Ratner has denied the allegations.) One attendee recalled that the Embassy seemed keen to avoid publicizing the affair: “We were specifically asked not to take any pictures or to post anything on social media.”
As a nepo hire on what
Le Figaro
has referred to as “the drunken ship of American diplomacy,” Kushner has often seemed less interested in winning over the French than in impressing the in-laws back in Washington. Ronald Neumann, the president of the American Academy of Diplomacy, told me, “I don’t see how he can possibly affect the opinions of the French government by regularly irritating them.” Even potential allies seem to regard Kushner warily. The former French President Nicolas Sarkozy, who has been tacking ever closer to the far right, revealed in a recent memoir that Kushner tried to visit him late last year in a Paris prison, where Sarkozy was confined for twenty days after being convicted of conspiring to fund his 2007 Presidential campaign with money from the late Libyan dictator Muammar Qaddafi. (Sarkozy is appealing.) Kushner told me that he was motivated by empathy. “I’ve been prosecuted, and my heart feels for the man,” he said. But the gesture seemed designed to cast doubt on the French judiciary’s verdict, suggesting that even a supposedly sovereign justice system was vulnerable to American meddling. Sarkozy confessed that he was “particularly surprised” by Kushner’s overture and uncertain how to handle it, wanting neither “to spark an unnecessary controversy” with his own country’s government nor to “turn away the representative of the world’s leading power while I myself was detained.”
In a new book, “Sous Influence Américaine” (“Under American Influence”), the CNN journalist Melissa Bell writes that the U.S. today is behaving like Russia, seeking to “destabilize, fragment, and vassalize Europe,” but that American interference can be even more insidious, “because it comes from a ‘friendly’ country.” Nathalie Loiseau, the chair of an ad-hoc European Parliament committee that aims to combat foreign interference, noted, as examples, the Trump Administration’s decisions to sanction the French bureaucrat Thierry Breton for his role in regulating American tech companies and to freeze the assets of Nicolas Guillou, a French judge on the International Criminal Court panel that issued arrest warrants for Israeli leaders. Magali Lafourcade, a French magistrate and the secretary-general of the National Commission on Human Rights, told me, “The idea is to say, ‘You’re under scrutiny, and you’re all at risk the moment you touch American interests.’ ”
Kushner is Trump’s man in Paris, but he is also a filial franchisee. One recent visitor to the Hôtel de Pontalba stumbled upon a supply closet filled with copies of “Breaking History,” Jared Kushner’s 2022 memoir, neatly labelled “Signed.” Last fall, the Embassy’s Instagram page posted a video of Charles pacing the ornate rug of a wood-panelled office with a phone to his ear. “POV: your son calls mid-meeting to tell you that he did it!” the caption read, touting Jared’s role in brokering a Gaza peace agreement. In “Breaking History,” Jared writes, of Arab leaders, “As the son-in-law of the president, and a former executive of a family business, I represented something that they found familiar and reassuring. They knew that when I spoke, I did so as an extension of the president in a way that few administration officials could.” Charles is an extension of the extension, burnishing the Kushner brand in the heart of Europe.
The Kushners’ longtime habit of mixing family and business has found new applications since they’ve entered the political realm. In 2018, when their real-estate firm, Kushner Companies, was in desperate need of a bailout for its over-leveraged purchase of a tower on Fifth Avenue, Jared traversed the globe, hobnobbing with world leaders as a senior White House adviser. At the last minute, an investment fund controlled by the Qatari government swooped in with the billion dollars that the Kushners needed. (The Kushners claimed that they hadn’t broken any ethics rules, because Jared had divested from the building, and that the deal had nothing to do with Trump’s subsequent efforts to negotiate an end to Gulf nations’ anti-Qatari blockade.) More recently, Jared’s private-equity firm, Affinity Partners, has raised billions of dollars from Middle Eastern governments as Jared serves as a U.S. envoy in the region.
The Kushner family business stretches back three generations, to Charles’s father, Joseph. He and Charles’s mother, Rae, were Polish Holocaust survivors who spoke often about the traumas they had endured. “There was seldom a family gathering or holiday meal in which it was not mentioned,” Jacob Schulder, one of their grandchildren, writes in a family history, published in 2024. Joseph had spent most of the war hiding in the forest with the Bielski partisan force, a Jewish resistance group. Rae, trapped in a ghetto in Novogrudok, watched the Nazis murder her mother and one of her sisters. She was forced to scour blood from the paving stones of the town square after a mass killing, accompanied by an orchestra. Eventually, after villagers dug an escape tunnel, she fled to the forest with the remainder of her nuclear family. Her brother, Chanan, became separated from the others and was never found.
Joseph and Rae spent several years in an Italian displaced-persons camp before immigrating to the United States. Kushner was Rae’s family name. As Andrea Bernstein writes in “American Oligarchs,” Joseph adopted it as his own and passed himself off as Rae’s father’s son, to more easily obtain a visa. After a few years in New York City, the couple settled in Elizabeth, New Jersey, where Charles, the third of their four children, was born, in 1954. He was named in honor of Chanan. Despite the family’s measure of suburban stability, money was tight. Joseph was transitioning out of the carpentry trade into real estate, and he and a partner were planning to build spec houses on three lots that they’d bought in Rahway. Jacob Schulder recounts that Joseph, cash-strapped from the purchase, “borrowed a hundred dollars from his uncle, Moshe, to make Charlie’s bris.” According to
New York
, when a young Charles came home from school one day with a guitar, Joseph broke it over his knee, saying, “A boy has to learn how to make a living, not play a fiddle.”
Joseph ultimately acquired some four thousand rental apartments in New Jersey. After his death, in 1985, Charles prevailed in a succession battle with his older brother, Murray. Armed with a law degree and an M.B.A., he transformed his father’s parochial holdings into Kushner Companies, amassing properties and investments. As his fortune grew, he took on a seigneurial role in the community, endowing yeshivas, underwriting World Series outings for sick children, and handing out prodigious political contributions, mostly to Democratic candidates. Masters of social capital, he and Seryl were ubiquitous at weddings and on the funeral circuit (they’d show up for the services, not just for the shivas) and were renowned for, as a family friend recalled, “taking care of their friends” while never forgetting a grudge. As major donors to pro-Israel causes, they got to know Benjamin Netanyahu, who once spent the night at their house, borrowing Jared’s bedroom.
Murray worked for the company, as did Charles’s two brothers-in-law (his sister’s husband and his wife’s brother). But in 2000, during a Passover Seder at the Fontainebleau hotel in Miami Beach, Charles and Murray clashed over a plan to buy another firm for more than a billion dollars; the deal had collapsed when Murray refused to sign off on it. The next year, again at the Fontainebleau, Charles lashed out at his sister, Esther, and her husband, Billy Schulder, whom he suspected of sympathizing with Murray. “You’re a fucking putz!” he screamed at Billy, according to
New York
, cementing one of the most consequential family feuds of the twenty-first century.
Kushner’s complicated web of interests had begun to attract the attention of federal authorities. In 2003, he learned that a grand jury was investigating him on charges of tax evasion and campaign-finance fraud—and that Esther and Billy were coöperating with investigators. Kushner, in a fury, devised the salacious revenge plot that has colored his reputation ever since. With the help of a moonlighting East Orange police captain and his private-eye brother, he recruited a sex worker to set a honey trap for Billy. The tryst was consummated at a motel called the Red Bull Motor Inn, where Kushner’s accomplices had installed a video camera inside a digital alarm clock.
The former New Jersey governor Chris Christie, who prosecuted Kushner’s case during his years as a U.S. Attorney, has called him “the most disgusting defendant” he encountered in his career. In Christie’s memoir, he describes how Kushner screened footage of Billy’s rendezvous in a conference room at his corporate offices, letting out “raucous guffaws.” Kushner wanted to show the tape to Schulder’s children—Kushner’s own niece and nephew—but ultimately settled for mailing a copy to the Schulders, timing the delivery so that his sister would receive it just before her son’s engagement party. In August, 2004, Kushner pleaded guilty to eighteen counts of tax fraud, witness intimidation, and F.E.C. violations. Six months later, he was sentenced to twenty-four months in prison. His reputation in shreds, he reported to a federal prison camp in Alabama.
Charles apologized for his actions, writing in a letter to his sister that he had “let hatred invade his heart” and had “committed a terrible sin,” but Jared never stopped believing that his father was a victim. His book, putatively “a White House memoir,” opens with Charles’s arrest, which Jared calls “an astonishing betrayal” on the part of his relatives. For years, he writes, he was traumatized by the smell of popcorn and Pop-Tarts, which were available in the vending machine of the prison’s waiting room. In February of 2006, after serving eight months, Kushner secured a transfer to a halfway house by claiming that he was an alcoholic.
That July, just weeks before Kushner’s return home, Jared paid ten million dollars to buy the New York
Observer
. One of Charles’s business associates told a reporter that the paper was a “graduation present” for Jared, but the purchase was very much a joint venture, guaranteeing entrée, for father and son, into a Manhattan world of very important people who didn’t much care about whatever the Kushners had got into across the river. “Charlie was a New Jersey criminal, so he needed a social reset,” the family friend recalled. A few years later, Jared married Ivanka Trump, at Trump National Golf Club, in front of five hundred guests, including Rupert Murdoch and Russell Crowe. The Kushners had arrived.
After Trump’s election in 2016, Jared and Chris Christie found themselves together on the Presidential transition team. Then Christie was abruptly fired, a move that he accused Jared of engineering as payback. Christie recently told me about an encounter with Charles, in the spring of 2023, at Fresco by Scotto, a clubby Tuscan restaurant near Rockefeller Center. Christie was there having lunch with the former New York governor Andrew Cuomo. “All the sudden, I see Cuomo’s eyes get bigger,” Christie recalled. “I felt someone pat me on the shoulder.” He turned around in his seat to find Charles Kushner standing behind him. According to Christie, despite the fact that he had sent Kushner to prison, the two men had never spoken.
“I knew it was over when my wife had bed bollards installed.”
Cartoon by Joe Dator
“Governor, I think it’s long overdue that we meet,” Kushner said to Christie. “My son has suggested that we get together for dinner.”
Christie interpreted Charles’s approach as a typically Kushnerian power play. “He and his son are carbon copies, and they have this very passive-aggressive style about them,” he said. “That was him hoping I’d be uncomfortable.” At the end of the encounter, Kushner held out a hand. “You can call me Charlie,” he said. (Through a spokesperson at the U.S. Embassy in Paris, Kushner characterized Christie’s account as “inaccurate.”) If nothing else, the incident demonstrated Kushner’s extraordinary capacity for the long game, for grinning and bearing anything that might eventually allow him to best an adversary. No get-together was ever arranged, but Christie told me that more recently, after he’d sat down at Ristorante MV, an Italian spot in Bernardsville, New Jersey, a server brought a bottle of expensive red wine to his table. “I told him, ‘I didn’t order any wine,’ ” Christie recalled. “He said, ‘Oh, no, sir, the wine was sent to you by your friend—Mr. Jared Kushner.’ ”
For both Republican and Democratic Administrations, the plush, well-staffed U.S. embassies of the major European capitals have traditionally served as parking grounds for big political donors who excel at schmoozing, if not at statecraft. Trump’s first Ambassador to France, Jamie McCourt, a G.O.P. fundraiser and a former co-owner of the L.A. Dodgers, took a look at the Hôtel de Pontalba’s lush garden, which abuts the Élysée Palace, in the heart of one of the city’s most historic districts, and, as aides recalled, asked if she could put in a pool. Kushner’s appointment to the Paris post was the most controversial since 1993, when Bill Clinton selected Pamela Harriman, a thrice-married Washington power broker who was ridiculed as a promiscuous gold-digger. During her confirmation hearing, Senator Strom Thurmond proclaimed, “They’re sending the Whore of Babylon to Paris!”
In the lead-up to Kushner’s arrival last summer, speculation about his agenda swirled in Paris. The French didn’t know what to expect. In one sense, the appointment was an insult. Géraud Araud, a French Ambassador to the United States during Barack Obama’s Presidency, wrote on X that Kushner, “needless to say, doesn’t have the slightest knowledge about our country,” and counselled followers to read Kushner’s résumé: “ ‘Juicy,’ as the Americans would say.” At the same time, Kushner’s proximity to Trump presented an opportunity. “It’s always better to have the ear of the President, no matter the Ambassador’s competence,” Célia Belin, the head of the Paris office of the European Council on Foreign Relations, told me. “The French actually love to deal with those kinds of Republicans, because their interests are laid out more simply, and they may actually be aligned on things like strategic autonomy.”
Kushner got to Paris on July 10th. The same day, he visited the Mémorial de la Shoah, noting afterward the “profoundly personal” nature of this “first step of my stay in France.” Just weeks later, he shared his impressions of the place in his open letter to Macron in the
Wall Street Journal:
“I write out of deep concern over the dramatic rise of antisemitism in France and the lack of sufficient action by your government to confront it.” Macron had announced his intention to recognize Palestinian statehood at the upcoming U.N. General Assembly, and Kushner wrote that Macron’s public statements on the subject had served to “embolden extremists, fuel violence, and endanger Jewish life in France.” His language closely echoed that of a letter Netanyahu had issued to Macron a week earlier. Kushner offered twinned reminders, one political and one personal. “Anti-Zionism is antisemitism—plain and simple,” he wrote, adding, “President Trump and I have Jewish children and share Jewish grandchildren. I know how he feels about antisemitism.”
The letter called out the very real problem of resurgent antisemitism in France. Since October 7th, antisemitic acts have soared, from fewer than five hundred incidents in 2022 to more than fifteen hundred in 2023 and again in 2024, with thirteen hundred and twenty acts reported last year. “There has truly been an explosion,” the historian Marc Knobel told me. According to one study, nearly a quarter of French people under the age of thirty-five consider it “acceptable” or “understandable” to vandalize a Jewish business or a synagogue in order to express opposition to Israeli policy. Kushner told me that he’d experienced antisemitism in France directly, when one of his grandsons was visiting and wore a yarmulke out for a walk during Passover. Kushner recalled, “We put one step out the door here—people yelling, ‘Fuck the Jew! Fuck the Jew!’ ”
David Amar, the president of the Consistoire de Paris/Île-de-France, an organization that oversees Jewish worship in the capital region, defended Kushner’s letter, telling me, “He simply said what everyone thinks aloud.” But, to many other leaders in France’s Jewish communities, Kushner’s claim that the French government had failed to act did not reflect reality. Responding on X to Netanyahu’s letter, Yonathan Arfi, the president of the Representative Council of Jewish Institutions in France, had praised “the regular dialogue established with public authorities against antisemitism over the past twenty years,” pointing to, for example, the government’s commitment to safeguarding Jewish places of worship. The lawyer Patrick Klugman, a longtime advocate for Jewish causes, told me, of Kushner’s intervention, “Theoretically, I should have been very pleased, but I was not, because it wasn’t serious, it wasn’t balanced, and it gave a false picture. Just because you’re not happy with what France is doing in the Middle East, you can’t say that the country is permissive to antisemitism.”
Kushner’s stunt, Klugman added, had put French Jews in an impossible position, awakening noxious stereotypes that reached back to the Dreyfus Affair. “It makes the Jewish population in France look as if they were not French but under American jurisdiction or protection, and this is totally counterproductive,” Klugman told me. If Kushner’s goal was to fight antisemitism in France, immediately alienating the country’s leadership and a significant portion of French Jews didn’t seem like a particularly efficient way to go about it. Nathalie Loiseau, the European lawmaker, said, “Sometimes you have to do undiplomatic things to have an effect, but the effect he had was most people teaming up against him and telling him to mind his own business.” (Kushner told me, “I think what I did was a net-net very positive, because nobody has the courage to say what I say, to express what I express.”)
The summons from Jean-Noël Barrot requested that Kushner appear at Quai d’Orsay, the seat of the French Foreign Ministry, the next day. These choreographies can be stagy, but most diplomats take them seriously, cognizant of the fact that they’ll need solid relationships in the event of a crisis, like, say, a terrorist attack. John Emerson, a former U.S. Ambassador to Germany who received his own summons after it emerged that Chancellor Angela Merkel’s phone had been tapped by the C.I.A., told me, “When you’re dealing with an ally, you go in and play your role. You respect their protocols. Otherwise, that disrespect becomes the story, instead of the message you want to deliver.” When Kushner didn’t show,
Paris Match
ran a piece headlined “The American Ambassador Prefers to Continue His Vacation,” with an accompanying photograph of Kushner on the French Riviera in a jaunty straw hat. He told me, of his decision to blow off the meeting, “I’m seventy-two years old. I’m not getting called to the principal at this stage in my life.”
The whole affair seems to have had little effect on Kushner’s sense of tact. Last October, he attended a
dîner mondain
—a networking dinner for people far too well placed to attend networking dinners—with luminaries from French business, culture, and journalism. It was hosted by James Lieber, a prominent consultant, at his apartment in Paris. The goal was to add social lubrication to the creaky wheels of diplomacy, but, according to several attendees, the conversation took a contentious turn. One guest told me, “Kushner started the dinner by saying that France was the main antisemite country of Europe, with Macron as the Antisemite-in-Chief.” (Lieber and the Embassy spokesperson denied that Kushner made these comments.) Eventually, the philosopher Bernard-Henri Lévy spoke up with an opinion that, per
Le Monde
, left Kushner in a “fury.” Lévy’s latest book, “Israel Alone,” argues that the October 7th attack prompted “a worldwide eruption of anti-Semitism, cloaked in anti-Zionism,” but, even for him, Kushner’s accusations went too far. According to the guest, “Lévy said, ‘
Quand même
, the letter you sent to the
Wall Street Journal
was quite tough.’ ” Kushner’s mood darkened as he replied, “No, it was actually very mild.” Lieber said that “the frank differences of opinion” were “only a brief part of an otherwise pleasant and interesting evening.”
Trump’s decimation of the federal bureaucracy, which included cutting thousands of jobs at the State Department, has triggered an unprecedented exodus from the Foreign Service. As of 2025, an estimated one-fourth of active officers had left the government altogether. Counting Guilfoyle’s vacated seat, ninety-three ambassadorial posts are currently unfilled, including in critical countries such as Germany and the United Arab Emirates. “It’s a big up-yours to the rest of the world,” Rubin, the former U.S. Ambassador to Bulgaria, told me of the vacancies. “And it’s a huge gift to countries like China, which never fails to fill their embassies overseas.”
Within the diminished ranks, Kushner is hardly the only Ambassador to run afoul of his host country. Not long before Guilfoyle’s resignation, the
Wall Street Journal
reported that she’d warned the Greek energy minister that the U.S. could topple governments in “any country we want.” In Canada, more than a quarter of a million citizens have signed a petition to remove Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, for, among other things, having “normalized the Trump administration’s threats to annex Canada as the ‘51st state.’ ” In Brussels, the Ambassador to Belgium, Bill White, was summoned by the government after publicly claiming that an Antwerp prosecutor’s investigation into ritual circumcisions by Jewish mohels without medical training was antisemitic. During an America 250 celebration that White hosted, police aggressively ejected a reporter and his editor after the reporter tried to ask White a question.
This new class of flamethrowing amateur diplomats has little reason to pursue the humdrum work of nurturing ties. Peter Ricketts, the former British Ambassador to France, told me, “I think the motivation of all these people is to get a good word from the boss. They don’t really care a fig how it’s received in the country they’ve been sent to.” Their provocations often feel like crude extensions of the American culture wars, as when the Ambassador to the Dominican Republic recently had a painting by Kehinde Wiley removed from the U.S. Embassy there, complaining that it depicted a “picnic” with “some lesbians.” The Ambassador’s partner in that endeavor was Erin Scavino, a former “Apprentice” star who now runs the State Department’s Art in Embassies program. According to
Puck
, Scavino, acting as a sort of
MAGA
art enforcer, has also targeted works such as a psychedelic glass sculpture featuring a horned figure and an infant’s impassive face, which was removed from the U.S. Ambassador’s residence in Bucharest after a G.O.P. congresswoman deemed it “satanic baby art.”
Such tactics dovetail with the Administration’s wider political objectives abroad, from establishing white victimhood to bolstering Israel and fighting the perceived weakening of Judeo-Christian values. Last year, at the Munich Security Conference, Vice-President J. D. Vance shocked Europeans by warning that the biggest danger to the Continent was not Russia or China but “the threat from within.” Soon after, Samuel Samson, a twenty-seven-year-old Deputy Assistant Secretary of State, expanded on the Vance doctrine in a manifesto, published on the State Department’s Substack account, titled “The Need for Civilizational Allies in Europe.” Across Europe, he wrote, “a decadent governing class afraid of its own people” was waging “an aggressive campaign against Western civilization itself.” Further evidence of the Administration’s attitude toward the Continent surfaced in a private Signal chat that had been formed just before the U.S. launched strikes against the Houthis in Yemen. Vance wrote, “I just hate bailing Europe out again.” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth found time to chime in: “VP: I fully share your loathing of European free-loading. It’s PATHETIC.” In the Trumpian mind, Europe is to the world as Manhattan is to America—an irksomely glamorous den of effeteness and decay.
Compared with Vance’s and Hegseth’s grudges, though, Kushner’s concerns about the Continent run deep. Less than a century ago, the Kushners were Europeans, too. Over the summer, he reportedly urged Trump to extend refugee status to French Jews, even as the White House was stripping Temporary Protected Status from hundreds of thousands of Haitian immigrants who’d fled catastrophe in their home country. The guest at the
dîner mondain
recalled Kushner remarking, with tears in his eyes, “The reason I’m here talking to you tonight is that my parents got wise enough to move to the United States.”
Among U.S. Ambassadors to France, domestic pot-stirring is not unprecedented. Charles Rivkin, an Obama appointee, wrote, in a leaked classified cable from 2010, that he intended to hammer France on the theme of “minority rights” and to challenge officials on “sacred cows” of French thought, such as the idea that universalism transcends ethnic and racial identities. What is different now is the scale, the stamina, and the straightforward ruthlessness of American obtrusions, and a sense that, as the transatlantic alliance deteriorates, the Trump Administration has made France a laboratory of interference.
Last year, for instance, soon after Kushner’s confirmation, Pierre Haski, the president of Reporters Without Borders, received an unusual visit, orchestrated by the American Embassy, from two State Department representatives. One of them, it turned out, was Samuel Samson, the author of the “Civilizational Allies” manifesto. The pair handed Haski business cards, emblazoned with golden eagles, and then started interrogating him about press freedom. The men cited, as the basis for their concern, the treatment of the far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who earlier that year had been found guilty of embezzling millions of euros in E.U. public funds to finance her political party, Rassemblement National (R.N.). According to
Le Monde
, the pair characterized her conviction as an authoritarian crackdown, and compared France to North Korea. Haski told me, “It was one of the most bizarre encounters I’ve ever had.”
“Would you like me to summarize this discussion?”
Cartoon by Dimitra Rizou
France is the European Union’s only nuclear power and its only permanent member of the U.N. Security Council. It is also home to the Continent’s largest Jewish and Muslim populations. Magali Lafourcade, the magistrate who heads the National Commission on Human Rights, told me that this makes France “the best country to attack in order to attack Europe.” Lafourcade had had her own off-putting encounter with the same duo who visited Haski. Again, the men’s questions focussed obsessively on Le Pen and her legal troubles. “They were very courteous and at the same time very intimidating,” Lafourcade recalled. The meeting left her alarmed enough that she reported it to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. She said, “I even went out to smoke a cigarette, and I don’t smoke—I felt so uneasy.” The incident preceded Kushner’s arrival in Paris, but it struck Lafourcade as a fitting prelude to his controversial public statements. The Administration’s tactics have reminded her of recent malicious acts in France tied to Russian operatives, such as the defacing of a Holocaust memorial with bloody handprints and the planting of a pig’s head outside a mosque. “It’s all to increase division and polarization,” she observed. (After Lafourcade discussed her encounter on television, her X account was suspended. She told me, “I perceive this as retaliation and a restriction of my freedom of expression.”)
The Presidential election, next May, will be of great consequence for France. After a decade in power, Macron cannot run again. His tenure has left a vacuum in the center, with a profoundly disillusioned French public gravitating toward extremes. Le Pen has been polling far ahead of any other candidate, and the recent unrest stands to strengthen her appeal among law-and-order voters seeking a vehement response. Amy Greene, a senior fellow at the think tank Institut Montaigne, told me that Trumpist actors view France as a “hopeful horizon” for a wider right-wing movement. “If such an economically powerful, nuclear power swings to the far right, then this is really a precursor for what the rest of Europe could look like,” she said.
In October, I returned to the Hôtel de Pontalba and met Kushner in the Samuel Bernard Room, a gilded salon named for one of Louis XIV’s bankers. After small talk about his properties in New Jersey, Kushner installed himself on a fauteuil upholstered in gold brocade. Seryl sat nearby, on a matching couch, facing three advisers. “I can’t sit on those sofas anymore at my age,” Kushner said. The air was suffused with the scent of freshly baked chocolate-chip cookies, which an aide proffered on a silver plate.
Several months into Kushner’s appointment, he had invited Le Pen and Jordan Bardella, the R.N.’s mediagenic young president, to the Hôtel de Pontalba. He then posted a photo of the three of them on X, writing that he “appreciated the chance to learn” from Le Pen and Bardella “about the RN’s economic and social agenda and their views on what lies ahead for France.” Trump has publicly backed the R.N., but for Kushner, a public servant singularly invested in combatting antisemitism, the French far right is an awkward ally. Marine’s father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, the founder of the movement, famously believed that the Nazi gas chambers were a mere “detail” of history. In recent years, the R.N. has remade itself as a champion of Israel, but I wondered whether the Party’s history bothered Kushner.
He told me, “I asked Marine Le Pen very directly, ‘Your father was a Holocaust denier. You have become, a generation later, a supporter of Israel. How did that light switch turn on and off so quick?’ She said it was a long time ago, and that she’d distanced herself from her father and his generation.” Kushner added, “I accepted that.”
In September, the French investigative outlet
Mediapart
unearthed antisemitic messages that Bardella had allegedly sent as a young R.N. adherent in the twenty-tens, including statements like “All the banks are owned by Jews.” (Bardella has denied sending the messages.) Kushner has met with representatives from center-left parties, but he told me that he has pointedly shunned Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s far-left party, La France Insoumise, over concerns about antisemitism in its leadership and its ranks. “I made it clear that blatant antisemites supported by the Muslim Brotherhood are not welcome in this residence, and whoever likes it, and whoever doesn’t, I don’t care,” Kushner said. But, when I brought up Bardella’s slurs, Kushner seemed untroubled.
“I know that he’s been to Israel, that he’s been very well received in Israel, and that he’s been very outspoken about being in favor of Israel,” he said.
“Would you receive him again here?” I asked.
“Yes,” he replied.
During our conversation, Kushner wavered between tough-guy talk and surprising delicacy. His views on Europe didn’t always align with the narrative of decline that his
MAGA
colleagues are pushing so vigorously. He told me that he had not witnessed much evidence of the “threat from within,” noting, “I don’t necessarily see it the way J. D. Vance sees it.” But he did share with his colleagues in Washington a capacious sense of the privileges of public office. After Sarkozy was released from prison, last November, Kushner finally met him, for lunch. As a further show of support, Kushner invited Sarkozy and his wife, Carla Bruni-Sarkozy, to his Fourth of July bash, and gave them a place of honor next to him and Seryl, with the Arnaults on the other side. Kushner told me that it was a “terrible slap in the face to France” to jail a President, “no matter what you did or didn’t do.”
“So is your idea that people in positions of power should not be put in prison or prosecuted?” I asked.
“I think if he shot somebody in the street, I’d feel different than if he had some nebulous dealing with some government,” he replied. Then he added, sounding miffed, “Ask me a fair question.”
An aide cut in to say that our time was up.
Kushner quickly recovered his bonhomie and said how proud he was “to represent our country.” Seryl began wrapping the untouched cookies up for me in napkins embossed with the ambassadorial seal. “I just got the coasters made,” she said. On my way out, the Kushners stopped by a side table, stacked with documents and tomes. “Do you have our son’s book?” Charles asked, handing me a copy of “Breaking History.” They insisted that I leave with more family mementos: a magazine with the face of their younger son, Josh, on the cover; a copy of a new children’s book co-written by Josh’s wife, Karlie Kloss, titled “Spaghetti Code: A Story About Problem-Solving, Pasta, and the Power of Big Ideas.” Speaking of their closeness to their kids and grandkids, all of whom live in the U.S., Kushner had told me, “It was a big sacrifice for us to come here.” He added, “We go back whenever we can.” ♦

epub_14.text:
By
Nick Paumgarten
Jim Morrison’s children finally appeared to him, seven years after their deaths, as he neared the summit of Mount Everest in the spring of 2018. He was climbing up the North Ridge, thirty minutes from the top, and he realized that they were alongside him, laughing and chattering in their familiar way. He began to laugh along with them, and then to cry.
Since losing his wife and kids, he’d been expecting that they would somehow reveal themselves. At the seaside, in the woods, up in the high alpine, he searched for a sign. Fishing a river, he waited for his kids to come out of the water. He imagined returning home from work to flowers on the table, or to a light mysteriously turned on. “This was a dream, a hope, and a desire, and because it never happened it caused me incredible grief,” he told me recently. “I concocted my own beliefs about life and death, and—energy. Their energy, who they really were, isn’t, or wasn’t, their body, their physical form.”
They had died when Jim’s wife, Katie Morrison, like him a pilot, was flying a single-engine turboprop Cessna, with the kids aboard—Wyatt, six, and Hannah, five—from Long Beach, California, to Henderson, Nevada, to visit a friend. A bad pocket of air over the desert caused the plane to plummet and crash.
Morrison, back home in Truckee, California, went to pieces. Each minute seemed impossible. The coroner strongly discouraged him from viewing the remains. His friends, most of them mountain people accustomed to untimely death, rallied around him. Sherry McConkey, whose husband, the freeskier Shane McConkey, had died a few years earlier, in a
base
-jumping accident, told me, “I was scared Jim would do something. I went to see him. He asked me, ‘What do I do?’ I said, ‘You’re fucked.’ ” She meant it as encouragement.
I first met Morrison in Puerto Rico, in the fall of 2018, when he buttonholed me at an athletes’ summit hosted by the North Face, the outdoor-gear company; the theme of the retreat, faddishly, was “storytelling.” I had been invited to tell stories about telling stories. “Do you want to hear my story?” Morrison asked. I wasn’t prepared for it. I was used to tales of avalanches and fatal falls, where the victims were inevitably people who had chosen to take the risks. The thrust of his telling, though, was of his recovery, amid a renewed, almost fanatical commitment to his lofty ambitions as a climber and a skier. He had discovered, during a hike soon after the tragedy, that the exertion went well with his tears. Endorphins altered the intensity of his grief, turning it into a twisted kind of exultation. The mountains became his balm.
On an expedition to Makalu, an eight-thousand-metre peak in the Himalayas, in 2015, he met the mountaineer Hilaree Nelson, who was freshly estranged from her husband, and they soon became inseparable, as lovers and as expedition partners—beasts of a similar nature and ability. Just before the Puerto Rico trip, Morrison and Nelson had successfully completed the first-ever ski descent of the Lhotse Couloir, the so-called Dream Line, a steep and unrelenting route from the peak just south of Everest. Now they were savoring their accomplishment with Nelson’s two preteen sons. On the second night of the summit, a few hours after Morrison told me his story, the team of athletes sponsored by the North Face held a ceremony to crown Nelson its new captain—an acknowledgment that, even in this assemblage of adventure all-stars, she was essentially the M.V.P.
Not long afterward, Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, fresh off winning the best-documentary Oscar for “Free Solo,” about the climber Alex Honnold, began shooting footage for a film about Nelson and Morrison—their lives together; their commitment to their craft, in spite of the risks and losses; and their project of all projects, a first-ever descent on skis of the north face of Everest. It was, as skiers say, the ultimate line, and something that Morrison had been dreaming about since he was a teen-ager.
The standard route up Everest is from the South Col, on the Nepal side; this is the source of those photos featuring long lines of snowsuited climbers gridlocked in the death zone. The north face is in Tibet, and the Chinese are strict about access. The route Morrison and Nelson had in mind, the Super Direct, via the Hornbein and Japanese Couloirs, has proved almost unclimbable, much less skiable. Only five people had ever reached the summit by that route. In such extreme terrain, a skier ideally wants to climb the line he is going to descend, to assess the snow. In 2002, a snowboarder named Marco Siffredi, who had ascended via another route, tried to descend the Hornbein. He dropped in and disappeared. His body was never found. No one had attempted it since.
The route is steep (up to sixty degrees), exposed (most of it in the “you fall, you die” category), punishingly long (nine thousand vertical feet), and prone to hellish conditions. During the usual climbing season, in the spring, there isn’t enough snow to ski on. The Hornbein is a flute of stone, with a thin ribbon of ice and snow. In the fall, after the monsoon, there is too much snow; constant avalanches make it suicidal to attempt. But Morrison and Nelson deduced that there might be a slim window, before the arrival of winter, when the avalanches have abated, leaving a firmer surface—skiable, if you have the chops and the guts.
Morrison and Nelson had both. Each of them had previously been to the summit of Everest—Morrison in 2018 (he’d skied part of the way down), Nelson in 2012 (she also reached the summit of Lhotse in the same twenty-four hours, setting a record). The pandemic interfered, but they picked other peaks, rehearsing for Everest, with the filmmakers along for the ride. On a 2022 trip to Manaslu, in Nepal, the cameras were there, recording the moment when Nelson, two turns into her run, got swept up in an avalanche and went over a mountainside. They were also there in the ensuing hours and days, as Morrison and his Sherpa companions searched the enormous debris field for her corpse. The recovery mission, involving remote, unexplored terrain, a helicopter at extremely high altitude, and the constant threat of more avalanches from above, was as dangerous, perhaps, as anything these men had ever attempted. But they shared the conviction, unusual for mountaineers in such a hostile place, that they couldn’t leave without her.
“It was a profound, transformational moment for me to know that when I found Hilaree, she wasn’t in her body,” Morrison told me. “I dug her out of the snow. I held her in my arms. I screamed, and I cried, but it was just her dead body. She was no longer there, and it was as clear as anything has been in my entire lifetime. I had been haunted so much by my wife and my children, and what state they were in when the plane crashed, and how they were recovered. I had been haunted by these visions of their half-burned corpses. Then contrast that with what I went through with Hilaree. There was so much more finality to it.” Morrison had her body cremated in Kathmandu, at a Buddhist temple.
“I had a happy childhood, but I was younger then.”
Cartoon by Kaamran Hafeez and Al Batt
The film project—and the Everest project—had changed. Cameras still rolling, Morrison, now doubly cursed, continued the quest without Nelson, while her boys, the ones I’d met in Puerto Rico, became motherless young men. It took three attempts, in the three years after Nelson’s death, to get it done. This is the heart of Chin and Vasarhelyi’s new film, “Everest: The Other Side,” which comes out this week.
Perhaps a spoiler alert is in order, but the news did travel far and wide last fall. On October 15th, Morrison’s team put a dozen climbers, including Chin and several of his film crew, on the summit, more than tripling the historical total of Super Direct summiteers in a single push. This time, it was Hilaree, rather than Wyatt and Hannah, whose presence came to Morrison on top, amid the summiteers’ celebration. He scattered some of her ashes, clicked into his skis, then set off toward the Hornbein, on the least hospitable snow he’d ever encountered. He took four hours to descend. A World Cup downhill race is two minutes. It’s hard to contemplate the burn, or the concentration, or the work and time and luck and loss that went into the effort. Here was four hours alone with the task, and with the sense that, if he fell, he’d consider his life to have been well lived. At the bottom of the face, he wept and shouted, in the conviction that he’d done right by Nelson, and by himself. But it would be a while before Morrison could get his own head around the accomplishment. “It dawned on me at a rate of about one per cent per day, for a hundred days,” he said. “But it was pretty damn satisfying, and it still is.”
Morrison has a house on Lake Tahoe, a trim three-bedroom that he renovated, stripping the drywall to expose stone walls and massive cedar beams. His friends call it the smallest house on the lake. Maybe so, but it’s good living. Glass doors open onto a patio, overstrung with prayer flags, a hot tub, a thin strip of lawn, and a dock. It was hard—looking out past the pier at the lake, with a full moon rising over Nevada—not to think of Michael Corleone, glowering in his parlor. While on Everest, freezing in his tent, Morrison watched “The Offer,” the TV series based on the making of “The Godfather.”
When I stayed with him one weekend last month, he also had as visitors Rob DesLauriers and his girlfriend, Merrill Joy. DesLauriers was one of the most prominent extreme skiers of my generation, a film star who also skied Everest via the South Pillar route, in a campaign, with his then wife Kit, to ski each continent’s highest peak, the so-called Seven Summits. (Jimmy Chin skied Everest with them.) DesLauriers, now a real-estate developer in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, officiated at the wedding of Chin and Vasarhelyi, in 2013. He was in town for a weekend of golf with his brothers.
“For a guy who doesn’t drink, that’s a pretty great bar,” DesLauriers said, pointing to a table stocked with fine liquor. Morrison, who is fifty-one, generally avoids alcohol, but he likes house guests, and host gifts. He’s tall and muscular, like an N.F.L. tight end, ruddy, rarely without a ball cap on a mostly hairless dome. He’d got a partial knee replacement four months before he went to Everest. During my visit, he had a deep cough that I mistook for a high-altitude croup, but it was just a whatever-phlegm, from weeks of glad-handing and travel for the film. He’d recently been the maid of honor at the wedding of the pro freeskier Michelle Parker. Friends say that in his younger years he was intimidatingly aloof, but now he has a serene, almost saintly air of self- possession—the product, one surmises, of calamity and achievement.
Large-format mountain photos hung on the walls around the house, but there were no photos of Morrison except for a small one by the kitchen sink of him and Chin, on the back of which Chin had written, “The Rest is Gravy. Everest ’25.” It was taken at the Rongbuk Monastery, in Tibet, the highest in the world. They stopped there, briefly, thirty-six hours after the descent. They had a flight to catch, and their Chinese minders were upset that Morrison wanted to linger at the monastery and light candles. “But I just skied the north face of Everest, so I can do what I want,” he told me. The monk inside, serving tea, seemed to recognize him and led him into the main monastery, a rare privilege, to meet the head lama, who, seeing Morrison, said, “Summit!” and mimicked with his arms the act of skiing.
“The Sherpa telephone,” DesLauriers said. “They always know everything.”
“We’d been focussed on this goal for six years,” Morrison said. “ ‘The rest is gravy,’ we kept saying. Then we came home, and I realized I wish I was at eight thousand metres again, trying to light the stove, just wondering if I could get this lighter lit.” Gravy, apparently, consisted of travelling, repeating himself in Q. & A.s, and meeting celebrities, to promote the film and the feat.
All he really wanted to do was go rock climbing. On Saturday morning, we met up with a bunch of his local friends at a gas station and headed up to a lesser-known crag. “It’s my favorite place here,” he said. The trailhead was twenty minutes up a rutted jeep track, through a creek and a pine forest. Forty-five minutes of hiking later, we were up on a ballroom floor of glacially smoothed granite which met a near-vertical wall some five stories tall. Jim Zellers, a pioneer of big-mountain snowboarding and a friend of Morrison’s for almost four decades, had for several years been bolting new routes on this face, refining and naming and grading. These days, Zellers stages events for the North Face; a few weeks before, he’d had the climbing team here for its annual meeting, but made the climbers promise not to identify the wall in their social-media posts. The others with us that morning were Sherry McConkey; Morrison’s frequent climbing partner Emi Kawakita, a Japanese Swedish woman from Stockholm; Shelton Gregory, a local contractor; Zellers; and Nick Russell, a professional snowboarder, who was leaving in two days for an expedition in Nepal. I trundled along, making excuses about not having climbing shoes, or any vestige of an abdominal core.
They paired up and warmed up on some less challenging pitches and then got to work trying to climb a route that had occupied their attention for months, called Jazz Hands, a 5.12b. “It’s the hardest I’ve ever done,” Morrison said. “It’s got it all.”
“It’s fifty-seven moves,” Gregory said.
“I lie awake at night thinking about it.”
“Me, too!” Gregory said. Picture Tahoe City’s middle-aged men, wide-eyed in the should-I-pee hour, shadow-climbing the same fifty-seven moves on the same granite face.
Gregory cued up some music on a speaker: a playlist (psychedelic cumbia) that he’d been spinning all summer, to the mounting annoyance of the others. It gave the proceedings a comic timbre. These hale adventurers lounging around an amphitheatre of granite: one could imagine they had it all figured out. They had modest but beautiful homes, gainful employment, health, free time, outdoor escapades. Then again, a quarter of their cohort was dead.
Soon it was Morrison’s turn on Jazz Hands, with Gregory belaying from the ground. He put on his shoes and chalked up.
“Today’s four years,” he said, half to the others, half to himself. His friends knew without his saying more that he meant it was the fourth anniversary of Hilaree Nelson’s death. “It’s Hil Day,” he said.
“Shane died on a twenty-sixth, too,” McConkey said. “So did Kip and Allison.”
“Sketchy day,” Morrison said. He put his hands on the rock. “Let’s see if I can manage not to fall.” He reddened with effort.
“When you do something really hard, it clears the brain,” McConkey said to me. “That’s why Jim is climbing mountains. We hold him. They held me. Everyone here is part of that death clan, which is pretty cool to have around you.”
The crag was in the shade. A crisp wind brought an autumnal chill. Everyone wore down puffers, which they took off when it was time to climb. Morrison had lent me one, and after a while I put my hands in the pockets. In the left one I felt a vial. Drugs? No. It was Hilaree—the last of her ashes, the rest having been scattered at the summit of Everest, a year before. I gave the vial to Morrison, and he walked over to a patch of brown grass at the base of Jazz Hands and, without any fuss or pomp, scattered the remainder of the ashes.
“Our next brew will be a collab with the chill dudes over at Long River Aleworks.”
Cartoon by Lars Kenseth
When Chin and Vasarhelyi’s film screened at the Telluride Film Festival, in Colorado, last month,
The Hollywood Reporter
published a withering review, calling it “a portrait of two reckless, ruthlessly self-involved people.” It referred to the climbers’ rationales as “selfish pablum” and to their “stunts” as “callous and cruel,” in light of Nelson’s leaving behind two children. (Chin was risking doing so, too.) Certainly, it is gutting, knowing what we know, to see Nelson onscreen addressing the possibility of death, and insisting on her right to pursue her ambitions. In the film, Vasarhelyi expresses dismay that her husband—the father of their two kids—is signing on for the Everest expedition, especially after so many of their friends have died.
“Let’s look at what the loss actually looks like,” she told me, regarding her intentions as a filmmaker. “I think about agency a lot. I have agency. Jimmy has agency. But the kids don’t.” (She and Chin are now getting divorced.)
Still, maybe these people aren’t reckless, any more than, say, astronauts might be, nor are they necessarily more callous toward their offspring than the law partner who works eighty-hour weeks or the celebrated artist who cycles through five wives. They’re adventurers, pioneers, limit testers, outliers, freaks. They are attempting to do the dangerous thing safely, as well as elegantly and uniquely, both for a living and for the nourishment of their souls. Their nutrients may not be yours. “To die is bad style,” a climber once told me. It is also inevitable. “There’s a cost to not taking risks, too,” Chin told me. “You can sit on your couch and eat chips until you have a coronary.”
Morrison has two professional careers and has thrived in both. He’s a skier and a home builder. These have more in common than you’d think, insofar as the culture of skiing has become the pretext for (and pretense behind) the kinds of houses he builds, and the kinds of clients he builds them for. As rugged mountain villages became, in the second half of the twentieth century, hubs of adventure sport—skiing, climbing, biking—they began to attract ever greater wealth. The dirtbags kicked off the cycle that eventually brought the new mega-West of log mansions, heated parking lots, and ersatz Frederic Remington oil paintings. The Rockies and the Pacific ranges are now latticed with ultra-fancy resort towns, with colossal lodge-like houses and high-end restaurants and shops. In the Lake Tahoe area, spread out as it is, the displays of extreme wealth may seem more diffuse than in the valley confines of Telluride, Aspen, and Jackson Hole. Still, they are abundant. The tech billions flow uphill from the Bay Area. The hills are alive with the sound of nail guns.
Many ski bums who stuck around became local grandees. The life style they personified served as advertising, in the way that artists and gay people colonize derelict urban neighborhoods and make them alluring to gentrifiers. The outdoor-apparel companies, by sponsoring athletes and films and catalogue shoots, converted derring-do into marketing fodder for developers and Realtors. Morrison has been on the front end and the back end, working the golden goose from tip to tail. He reckons that he has built about a hundred luxury homes in the area.
Morrison was born in Pittsburgh but reared in Walnut Creek, California, a suburb in the East Bay. His father was an electrical engineer at Westinghouse. Morrison caught the mountain bug when he was twelve, at the local gear store, Sunrise Mountaineering; his mother, a manager at a law firm, was buying him a water bottle and some hiking boots for a Boy Scout backpacking trip. He was transfixed by the climbing tools hanging from the walls, and by the photographs of the store’s owners scaling snowy peaks in Alaska. He did a little research and learned that people climbed on Mount Diablo, nearby. “I went to the store and talked to the employees there and read books and learned about it,” Morrison said. “And eventually I got to Mount Diablo, and I set up my own top rope, with my own equipment, with nobody else. And I did my own rappels.” He practiced out of his bathroom window, on the second floor of the family tract house. “I made an anchor on my toilet. Now I’m a contractor—you realize that a toilet is fastened by two little bolts. It’s basically just sitting there.”
On weekends, he skied at Lake Tahoe, first at Alpine Meadows, then on the mogul team at Squaw Valley (which was renamed Palisades Tahoe six years ago). Like many groms of his generation, he had a V.H.S. copy of the Greg Stump ski film “The Blizzard of Aahhh’s,” and watched it every day for a year. The summer after his junior year of high school, he arranged to go to New Zealand for a mogul camp. To raise the necessary funds—he wasn’t earning enough in his job, as a stock boy in the women’s-shoe department at Nordstrom—he biked around Walnut Creek with a stencil kit and offered to repaint residents’ sun-faded addresses on the curbs in front of their houses, at ten bucks a pop. After a showdown with the president of a homeowners’ association, he finagled a contract to do the whole subdivision, which got him the sum he needed for the trip. “My parents, while I was gone, read my yearbook and saw all these notes from friends that were, like, ‘We should do bongs this summer,’ ” Morrison said. “And they were, like, ‘What the heck is happening? Who are you? What is wrong with you?’ ”
What was really wrong with him, though, was that he had begun to cultivate the idea of climbing and then skiing down the world’s biggest mountains. He already had eyes for the north face of Everest and the Hornbein Couloir. He dropped out of college, moved to Chamonix, France, the epicenter of alpinism, and began to level up, knocking off semi-obscure first descents in order to make a name for himself. He was competing on the international extreme-skiing tour and was sponsored by some of the top gear companies. Then, his second winter there, he blew out a knee.
He flew back to Tahoe and moved in with his parents, who had a house share there. On his first night without crutches, he went to a party because his older brother, John, who was also a skier, had told him that the marketing director of the North Face would be there. She was not, but, as he sat alone, rubbing his knee, a woman—Katie—approached him and started razzing him about nursing his injury. They began to flirt. Two years later, they were married. Morrison, in her thrall, put aside his skiing career and his inchoate dreams of Everest, and instead, with his characteristic intensity, tried his hand at home construction.
The first project was putting on a deck, which earned him three thousand dollars. “So now I had a net worth of three thousand and forty bucks,” he said. He knew a local real-estate agent who was marketing a new development, with thirty-five buildable lots. Morrison found a partner who would pay for one of them. Morrison would build the house and get twenty per cent of the equity. The catch was that he didn’t actually know how to build a house. Zellers poured the foundation, and Morrison hired fellow ski bums to do the framing, masonry, and tiling. For a while, he was operating under the contractor’s license of his former mogul-team coach. Across the street, Ernst Hager, a national-ski-team coach and an operations guy at Squaw Valley, was building a house at the behest of the same real-estate agent. Morrison visited the site regularly and studied Hager’s work. “I was learning how to do it the day before I did it,” Morrison said. “Like, ‘Why is there glue in all these joists?’ ‘Well, you put glue in the hangers so they don’t squeak.’ The next morning, I told my crew, ‘We need glue for the joists.’ ‘Glue? Why?’ ‘So the hangers don’t squeak.’ ”
Morrison was twenty-four years old. He met his parents for dinner to tell them about his new career. “All they did was try to talk me out of it,” he said. “My father always used to talk about hard work, how nothing comes for free. ‘Money doesn’t grow on trees,’ he said. ‘You’ll see.’ But when I saw this lot, in that development, I thought, This is money growing on trees.”
Ten years later, Morrison had two kids and a thriving construction business that was building several houses at a time. The family was living in Lahontan, a high-end gated community on a golf course, in Truckee. “I was the youngest member there, by a long shot,” he said. “I’d made a lot of money at this point. And I was leveraging all of it into the houses. Build a house, make it work, sell it, do it again.” The family moved in and out of his builds. “My daughter lived in five houses by the time she was five years old.”
One night, when Katie had flown down to Los Angeles, he called her and said, “Honey, this business is cranking, our kids are in a great place, we’re really going to do this.” They had a plan to spend part of the year in Chamonix, enroll the kids in school there. “I had the world by a string,” he told me. “I thought we had it all.” And then, the next day, they were gone.
After a second day of climbing, Morrison, in his Chevy pickup, took me on a tour of some of his building projects. He brought me to a newer gated community, called Martis Camp. “It’s Lahontan on steroids,” he said. Two thousand acres, almost seven hundred lots, snug against the Northstar ski area, with views of the Martis Valley and the Sierra Crest. The golf course, glimpsed through the pines, was unexpectedly lush. “I’ve built, like, seventy-five houses in here,” Morrison said.
During the 2008 financial crisis, most of the construction at Martis Camp came to a virtual halt. But Morrison kept going, despite being leveraged to the hilt. Now, as he navigated the winding blacktop roads, past monstrosities both ultra-modern and outré-Montana, he told the story of his financial survival—the cunning, the bravado, the near-disasters—and it was as harrowing, in its way, as any expedition in the Himalayas. Still, one wouldn’t expect it to become a Chin and Vasarhelyi
IMAX
spectacular anytime soon.
He pulled up at a house he’d finished in the spring for two Bay Area investors, brothers. It was ten thousand square feet, three years in the making, and, although he wouldn’t tell me how much he got paid for the job, it was obvious to me, after years of hate-reading the Mansions section of the
Wall Street Journal
, that this house had to be worth tens of millions of dollars. It was what you might call deep Vail-core: heavy stone, big wood, big glass. An immaculate garage had a fleet of bicycles and golf carts and kids’ scooters. We removed our shoes and went from room to room. Muscular floorboards of stained oak, with wooden pegs; massive steel posts and beams clad in a veneer of reclaimed wood; florid paintings of cowboys and bears; excellent whiskeys and patios and books; a stone fireplace the size of a lighthouse. Say what you will about the taste, but the work was very fine. “There are ninety-six pieces of wood in this column,” Morrison said. “Seven hundred or so pieces of wood in this room.” Here and there was custom metalwork fashioned by the burly homeschooled guy from Vermont who earlier that day on the crag I’d seen climb a 5.12d+, and whose shoes I’d borrowed to get a taste of a 5-point-much-less. Side-by-side desks stood in the brothers’ office. One held the business book “Margin of Safety,” and the other held “Brave New World.”
Driving back to his house, we were talking about marriage, or, really, about some of our friends’ marriages. There had been a run of divorces in his mountain set. He recalled visiting Katie’s family in northern Michigan, when he and Katie first started dating, and seeing her parents in the back of a boat, cuddled up under a blanket, giggling. “They were so in love with each other,” he said. “That’s what I want.” He’d had it and lost it twice. “I’m either doing that, or I’m not doing it at all.”
Recently, Morrison had found himself in another kind of relationship, one that was as nourishing to him as it was baffling. Of all the crazy things that had befallen him since skiing Everest—Prince Harry buying him rounds, Meghan Markle texting him on the crag, dining with John Malkovich—one stood out. Speaking in Los Angeles at a conference organized by Jeffrey Katzenberg, he was invited on a podcast with Oprah Winfrey. She had followed the Everest triumph but had had no idea about the tragedies he’d endured. Morrison was taken by her energy, her presence. “It was just a tremendous amount of similarities in our passion, in our lives, and in how we have manifested our own outcomes through hardship,” he told me. “I was just, like, I love this woman.”
They exchanged numbers and made plans to meet in Telluride, at the première of the Everest film. She had a house there, and he had one, too, which he’d originally built to live in with Nelson and her sons. (He sold it over the summer. Telluride got a little weird for him: Hilaree’s town, without Hilaree. “Every time I went to get groceries, it was, ‘Are you O.K.? Are you
really
O.K.?’ ” He got a house in Aspen, instead, but still sees and keeps in touch with the boys.) He and Winfrey went for dinner in town. She began planning a party for him and the film. “I’ve never had a party at my house before,” she told him.
Tent, band, flowers: everything just so. “It was essentially a wedding for me,” Morrison said.
“A part of my soul was stirred by him,” Winfrey told me. “It makes me tear up to think about him. He’s one of the most extraordinary people on the planet. Here’s a guy who can have joy and grief existing in the same heart.” For the party, she had him write something that she could print on a four-by-six-inch card and leave at each place setting; she also read it aloud to the guests.
When Morrison told me about all this, we were sitting at his kitchen table, still in our clothes from the crag. Night had fallen on the lake. The conversation would go on deeper into the night—“I’m an endurance athlete,” he’d say—but at this moment he stood and fetched a tawny box, made of paper from Nepal, tied up in twine, and began gingerly unwrapping it. Inside was one of the cards, which bore twenty-two lines, center-formatted on fine grainy stock, his signature at the bottom.
I read it to myself, as one does, in my inner Oprah voice: “The mountains have given me so much. They’ve also taken a great deal from me. I don’t climb or ski for the risk. I do it for the presence it demands.” Then I handed it back, and he put it aside to wrap it up again. “I was going to give this to my mom,” he said.
It was tempting to think of this as another node in the grief-industrial complex, the gyre of thrills and kills, sentiment and content, but the force of Morrison’s belief, his tenacity and quietude, and the way it seemed to reflect what little I knew about those characteristics in Winfrey, made me feel suddenly and resolutely happy for him. This was when he began to tell me about encountering the spirits of his children on the North Ridge. ♦
