In a consulting room, Rau was seeing the patient from California. The setup was, at first glance, like any doctor’s: medical degrees on the wall, an examination table at the center. But I also noticed a small silver machine in a corner, called a
Vegatest
II, which measures changes in a patient’s electromagnetic fields, purportedly to ascertain sensitivity to certain toxins. It had knobs—one was marked “Provokation”—and a display with a needle that went from zero to one hundred, like an old-fashioned laugh-o-meter. Rau explained that he had just used the
Vegatest
II to investigate the harm done by toxins that had “leached” from the patient’s silver-amalgam fillings. In a 2018 documentary about the alleged dangers of root canals, “Root Cause,” Rau was quoted as saying that ninety-seven per cent of his breast-cancer patients between the ages of thirty and seventy had had “a root canal or toxic situation in the teeth.” (The film received fierce criticism from the American Dental Association, and Netflix, which had been streaming the documentary, pulled it.)
The Californian had short dark hair and carried a thermos from the luxury spa Canyon Ranch. I was invited in after she’d finished a colonic irrigation. (“I draw the line at that one,” she told me.) The patient, who was in her early fifties, told me that she’d developed multiple myeloma in her early forties. She’d had two bone-marrow transplants and was advised to undergo maintenance chemotherapy. She refused and instead began treatment under Rau, who focussed on ozone therapy and on removing gluten from her diet. Her multiple myeloma did not recur. “It sounds so kitschy,” she said. “But he’s basically saved me.” She now made a yearly visit to BioMed, where her regimen included multiple injections. “Only two today?” she asked, surprised. (She once received twenty-seven injections in a single session, she recalled.) She said, of one admixture, “They call it the tumor infusion—it’s specifically for people with cancer. Don’t ask me to tell you what’s in it. The ampules are always in German.”
Rau also gave her a dark-field-microscopy screening. “Look at all the rouleaux,” the Californian said, clearly upset. Rouleaux, in the vocabulary of dark-field microscopy, are blood cells that are stacked like pancakes. In theory, such an arrangement diminishes the cells’ ability to transport oxygen from the lungs. But Rau was preoccupied with another problem: images from the screening indicated that she was in a state of “hyper-proteinization.” The Californian was contrite. “We went to Italy for four days, and I wasn’t vegan or gluten-free,” she confessed. “But I’m back on it. I bet it will improve.”
“Look here—it’s not so bad,” Rau said, consolingly. “The cells, they move.”
On April 13, 2021—the day after Lanitis died—the Appenzell Ausserrhoden prosecutor’s office ordered the seizure of relevant records and called for an autopsy, which revealed that Lanitis had died of multiple organ failure.
Around this time, Kotthaus, Rau’s colleague, wrote to Lanitis’s daughter, Manglis, saying that she was “heartbroken.” Manglis asked what, exactly, had caused her mother’s organs to fail. Kotthaus answered that it was disseminated intravascular coagulation—a blood-clotting disorder. Manglis told me that her family secured a lawyer “pretty fast.”
The Lanitis family was warned that a toxicology report might be slow in arriving—the substances in Lanitis’s body were not the sort that the canton’s forensic scientists typically evaluated. After nearly a year, a report on Lanitis’s death was finally released to the family. It noted that the clinic had used alpha-lipoic acid in an off-label manner, and possibly without providing adequate information to the patient, which is required in Switzerland. By then, prosecutors had raised the possibility that the infusions had been contaminated. They were sent off for special testing at the hospital in St. Gallen. Nothing was found. This meant that the pharmacist who had prepared the I.V.s was not at fault—and that Rau and Kotthaus remained the main figures of judicial interest.
Manglis had started Googling Rau to see if he had a history of problematic outcomes. She eventually found Swiss newspaper articles, in German, about Sadruddin Aga Khan. Suddenly, Manglis said, she was confronting “the possibility that this doctor has been losing patients for a long time under suspicious circumstances.” She added, “I felt like I bore some responsibility for not vetting my mother’s medical choices.”
Before the two doctors were scheduled to testify in the inquiry, the prosecutor’s office called in a woman named Vera Torosian, who had been a naturopath at BioMed during the period in question. Torosian had been working in the United States, and Rau hired her in the hope that she would attract American patients to the clinic. She had no animus toward Rau, she testified, but from the beginning she was skeptical of many of the techniques she observed at BioMed. For instance, she saw patients being sent to the hyperthermia machine even though they seemed too weak to endure extreme heat. A few days after Lanitis’s death, Torosian called the police. (In her testimony, she recalled struggling “for a long time beforehand about whether to do it.”) She was directed to the prosecutor’s office, where she laid out her concerns—including an incident that she found alarming. Torosian, who left BioMed soon afterward, claimed that she’d seen a Swiss patient in the waiting room who was so weak that she could barely stand. The woman had been getting various treatments, including repeated sessions with a
papimi
—a device, not approved by the F.D.A., that applies high-intensity, short-duration electromagnetic pulses to the body. The woman ultimately died of advanced cancer.
One patient that Torosian had introduced to Rau was a friend named Mary Anne Hawrylak, an American who owned a medical-services company. Hawrylak was not a hard-core believer in alternative medicine, but she prided herself on keeping an open mind. She had suffered from an excruciating autoimmune disorder decades earlier, and she wanted to take steps to prevent its recurrence. “I’m interested in things beyond standard of care, because standard of care doesn’t always address things beyond just the symptoms,” she told me. After discussing her condition with Rau, she signed up for a three-week stay at BioMed.
Her visit overlapped with Lanitis’s, and they became friendly. They had meals together and chatted about their children and grandchildren. They planned an excursion to St. Gallen.
On April 9th, a few hours before Lanitis received her infusion, Hawrylak herself underwent an alpha-lipoic-acid treatment. When I asked her about the various infusions she received at BioMed, she said that she had asked Rau about them, and that he had said very little. “He never told me the ingredients,” she said. “And, had he told me the ingredients, I might not have known what that meant, anyway, unless he said, ‘Here are the potential side effects.’ ” (Rau says that all of his patients are given consent forms.)
After receiving the alpha-lipoic acid, Hawrylak felt confused and dizzy. She went to her hotel room to lie down. “Honestly, I thought I was going to die,” Hawrylak remembered. Torosian encouraged her to go to the hospital, but Hawrylak refused:
COVID
rules were in force, and Hawrylak, who doesn’t speak German, was scared that she would have to enter the emergency room alone. A while later, Rau tested Hawrylak’s platelets and found that they were slightly reduced.
In the meantime, Lanitis had fallen seriously ill. After Jeff Höseler, the hotel manager, told Hawrylak that her friend had been taken to the hospital, Hawrylak asked Rau, “Is she going to die?” Rau said that it didn’t look good.
Rau, wondering if his patients had been poisoned somehow, had his staff check the kitchen for contamination. He went to the infusion room and found the used ampules of alpha-lipoic acid in a biohazard-waste container. He tested some remaining drops and found no problems. Rau wondered whether the women’s
COVID
vaccines had caused them to have adverse reactions to the acid. A month before Lanitis died, she had received the AstraZeneca vaccine, which has been linked to problems with blood clotting at a rate of one case in every hundred thousand. Hawrylak, however, had been given the Pfizer vaccine, which has not been strongly implicated in any blood-clotting issues.
Rau called the hotel’s guests to a wood-panelled library where copies of “The Swiss Secret” were on display. He announced that a patient had been given an infusion and subsequently died. There would be no more such treatments until he could rule out the infusion as the cause. The guests seemed less upset by the death than by the news that their infusions would be halted. Hawrylak remembers their response as “We paid so much money—we want these infusions.” She told me, “I thought I was in ‘The Twilight Zone.’ ”
Hawrylak was shocked when Rau told the guests that other patients had been given the same treatment and had not been harmed. “I looked at him and he gave me a weird look,” she told me. (Rau disputes this.) She was so angry that she took a walk in the snow to gather her emotions.
Hawrylak soon left. She said goodbye to another friend she’d made at BioMed, a British woman with cancer. She did not warn the woman that Rau was untrustworthy. “I didn’t want to talk to her about it, because she had just complete faith in this,” Hawrylak told me. “And the last thing I want to do is shake somebody’s faith.”
Torosian’s testimony stunned Manglis and her family. “It’s the first time I’m understanding the extent of what’s happening,” Manglis told me. She now knew that her mother and Hawrylak had been given the same infusion on the same day and that both had appeared to have had strong adverse reactions. A possible reason that Hawrylak had survived was that she was physically larger than Manglis’s mother, who was petite. The earlier death of Ammann—who weighed little more than a hundred pounds upon her final arrival at BioMed—was consistent with this hypothesis.
Gossip was swirling at the clinic. Torosian had told the prosecutor’s office that an undernourished, severely disabled girl who was receiving treatment at BioMed was subsisting entirely on spinach—on Kotthaus’s orders. After learning of this and other allegations, Rau and Kotthaus each sued Torosian for defamation. (They lost these suits, but Kotthaus told me that the accusation about the disabled girl was “bullshit.”)
Eventually, Höseler was contacted by the police, and afterward he began exchanging texts on WhatsApp with Zacharie Tachi, an employee at the hotel’s restaurant.
“This is getting tight for Dr. Rau,” Tachi texted.
“I can’t really remember who all died, names and number of deceased, do you still have them in your head?” Höseler wrote.
Tachi said that he couldn’t remember any names.
Höseler speculated about several such deaths. There was “the Zurich woman”—Ammann. “The lady from Cyprus”—Lanitis. A “lady from Germany.” A “lady from Slovenia.” Rau told me that these texts reflected medical ignorance: the last two women had come to him terminally ill. (The prosecutor’s office opened a separate investigation into allegations of mistreatment and additional deaths at the clinic and identified no criminal misconduct. The case against Rau has remained limited to Lanitis and Ammann.)
Like Torosian, Höseler left his job, and he later shared his texts and other evidence with prosecutors. The restaurant in the Sonnenberg, he told them, was meant to be a place of “joie de vivre.” But Rau’s arrangement was “a money-making machine with the potential to save lives but not to bring joy.”
In May, 2023, the prosecutors finally interrogated Kotthaus and Rau. Kotthaus attended the hearing but declined to answer most questions. Rau spoke more freely. He said that he didn’t remember much about Lanitis—Kotthaus had been the doctor in charge and had done most of the interfacing. But, to indicate how seriously he had taken the incident, he noted that this was “the first time in my life” that he had driven a patient to a hospital himself. He did not deny that Lanitis’s death might have been related to the alpha-lipoic-acid infusion or to other treatments she’d received, though he cautioned that “the causal connection seems to have been drawn a bit too hastily.”
On November 18, 2023, the Sunday edition of the Swiss newspaper
Neue Zürcher Zeitung
published an investigation into the deaths at BioMed, written by a reporter named Leo Eiholzer. It laid the blame mostly on Rau, who brought legal action against the paper, demanding to be allowed to publish a rebuttal in its pages. (A judge denied his suit.) After the article ran, canton officials invited Hawrylak to fly to Switzerland and recount her experience to prosecutors.
Rau, in his first round of testimony, seemed to acknowledge having used alpha-lipoic acid off-label. And he entertained the notion that he should more explicitly inform patients about the potential risks of such treatments. “That has nothing to do with the causality with the tragical cases,” he said. “But I can see the point.” In his second round of testimony, he took a tougher tack. He insisted that the infusion was completely appropriate. Lanitis’s toe bursitis had been accompanied by “subtle neurological problems,” and to him this seemed to be “a classic indication for the infusion.” He said, “It’s too narrow to say that just because she hasn’t had diabetes it’s not indicated.”
Later in this testimony, Rau claimed that it was unreasonable to expect him to inform patients “about complications that practically never occur.” All the same, he emphasized, he
did
take his duty of care very seriously, especially when using medicines off-label. Indeed, he had personally reported Lanitis’s death to the canton. “If I had wanted to cover something up, I certainly wouldn’t have done that,” he said.
The prosecutor then turned to the death of Ammann. Both sides dug in hard here. The postmortem report, which was conducted by an expert at the Zurich hospital, found that Rau had mishandled Ammann’s case from the start. He had missed clear signs of intestinal paralysis, which can lead to sepsis, and had failed to respond to severe gastrointestinal bleeding, which can occur in someone with an abnormally low platelet count. Rau should have sent her to a surgical clinic; cases like hers have “an excellent success rate and survival prognosis.” The report called BioMed’s diagnostic efforts “incomprehensible.” It concluded that Rau had breached “the doctor’s duty of care.” (Rau disputes this report and commissioned a counter-expert opinion that challenged the report’s assessment about the cause of Ammann’s death.)
Rau called the allegation that he’d missed an intestinal issue “nonsense”—the day after he gave Ammann the infusion, he’d placed a stethoscope on her abdomen and heard normal digestive activity, and he was further reassured when she ate and didn’t vomit. In addition, he said that Ammann had nerve inflammation, which in his view was more or less peripheral neuropathy—a condition for which alpha-lipoic acid is approved in Germany. The question of whether the infusion caused Ammann’s death was more complex than in Lanitis’s case, because none of the acid remained in Ammann’s blood at the time of her death, nearly three days after the treatment. (Melissa Gittinger, a medical toxicologist, told me that the substance passes through the system “in hours.”) But the fact that Ammann’s platelet count, like Lanitis’s and Hawrylak’s, had been impacted after the alpha-lipoic- acid infusion suggested that Ammann, too, might have had an adverse response.
Rau testified, of Ammann’s case, “In our opinion, this death is still completely unclear.” His late friend, he said, had had various problems with her inner milieu, including a history of “heavy-metal contaminations.” Rau said that he doubted Ammann had screamed in pain—the Doris he knew was too suave for such an outburst. The prosecutor later asked him why her partner would make such a detail up. Rau couldn’t say.
As to why it had taken so long for Ammann to be sent to a hospital, Rau said, it was in part because she was famous in Switzerland and shy of publicity. Moreover, he added, “trying to prove whether time was lost here is just a matter of finding someone to blame.” At one point, he protested, “I’m a good internist.” The charge of “negligence,” he went on, “hurts me. I’m not a negligent doctor. That’s why I have many patients from all over the world.”
In January, 2025, Rau gave prosecutors a written defense of his actions. He insisted that the Swiss woman whom Torosian had found in the waiting room had not been mistreated, pointing out that her family had thanked him in the woman’s obituary in the St. Gallen newspaper. The woman, whose family did not want her to be named, had died of advanced cancer. But, when I reached the woman’s husband, he said that Rau “didn’t act as a doctor but as a business partner.” Although he said that Rau had given his wife a good final month, he wondered if she might have lived longer if she hadn’t left standard care: “She simply blocked conventional medicine, and that’s actually Rau’s business model—he grabs her and says, ‘Yes, come to me.’ ”
Rau told me with pride that many of his patients came back more than once—he affectionately called them “repeaters.” Manglis saw this differently. “Part of the grift is to keep you coming back,” she said. But others I spoke with insisted that Rau was a master diagnostician. Xenia Lehner, a nursing specialist in St. Gallen who worked at BioMed for a year, and at Paracelsus before that, wrote to me, of Rau, “Both he and Dr. Kotthaus were providing much care and quality in their treatment—probably the main reason why patients follow them.”
In October, 2022, Ammann’s sisters filed a criminal complaint accusing Georg Frei of failing to get her to a hospital promptly. “This situation should have filled a life partner with great fear,” it said. Rau’s lawyer has noted that Frei stood to inherit two properties and nearly fifty million dollars upon Ammann’s death. This past March, a prosecutor dismissed the complaint, finding that Frei had acted in a sufficiently “timely manner” and had taken “the measures that could reasonably be expected of him.”
When Torosian, the naturopath, testified for a second time, in February, 2025, Rau’s attorney made a shocking insinuation. After questioning Torosian about an F.B.I. course in criminal investigative analysis she had taken, he implied that she might have poisoned the victims with arsenic. This stratagem went nowhere: when he asked her to confirm that a person with her expertise would know how to disguise arsenic poisoning, there was “tumult” in the courtroom and the question was declared inadmissible. Moreover, Torosian claimed that she had never administered
any
substances at BioMed. All the same, prosecutors requested an expert report on arsenic poisoning, which caused further delay.
This past March, the Appenzell Ausserrhoden prosecutors finally charged Rau and Kotthaus with two counts of negligent homicide and sent the case to a judge for a trial. In Switzerland, a trial is a much smaller, more compact affair than in the United States. The proceeding often takes place in a single day. But it has still not been scheduled and may not happen for many months.
Earlier this year, after the prosecutor signalled that he intended to stop collecting evidence and file charges, Rau’s lawyer demanded that the prosecutor recuse himself, claiming that he was “trampling on Dr. Rau’s right to evidence.” Rau plans to submit his counter-expert report on Ammann’s death for the trial, and continues to plead his case—he recently produced an annotated hundred-and-fifty-page chronology of events relating to her case, in which he describes her having various maladies, including a hormonal imbalance and chronic inflammatory-bowel disease. He also sent me a shorter document about the death of Lanitis, saying that he didn’t know why she died and calling for the case to “be assessed by a truly independent, interdisciplinary expert review.”
The prosecutor has asked for a suspended fourteen-month prison sentence for Rau and a ten-month one for Kotthaus. A licensed psychiatrist, Kotthaus has started her own practice in the nearby town of Herisau, focussing on “body/mind” medicine. Kotthaus feels that she and Rau are being scapegoated for practicing alternative medicine: “The things the emergency-room doctors wrote down in Herisau, in St. Gallen . . . it’s, like, prejudiced. Since we don’t do mainstream medicine, we do harm. We do not know what we are doing.”
Whatever happens in court, the canton could try to prohibit the two doctors from practicing medicine. But Rau is an eminent figure in the area, and Andreas Dudli, a lawyer for the Lanitis family, told me, “I’m not sure if they have the courage to take away his license in this tiny canton.” Rau’s lawyer told me he was prepared to appeal the case all the way to the European Court of Human Rights.
Manglis hopes for a guilty verdict, in part, to warn patients away from BioMed. She said recently, “I think a lot about how, when I spoke to my mother the day before she died, she was so confused about what was happening to her.” It still made no sense to her that her mother’s visit to a serene alpine retreat had ended in painful sudden death. “It feels like I’m often occupying that same state—the state of ‘What the fuck happened?’ ” ♦
An earlier version of this article misstated Evie Lanitis’s age when she arrived at BioMed and mischaracterized Thomas Rau’s remarks about the other doctors who treated Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan before his death.

Fiction
Wall Cano
By
Souvankham Thammavongsa
Illustration by Lewis Chamberlain
Mom left. Dad didn’t tell us anything. He just got up, and dressed, and told us to eat something. I saw some bananas on the kitchen counter with a few freckles on them and tore one from the bunch. Dug a nail through the end and peeled its yellow skin off. It came away in strips, three thick strips. I looked for bruises. I can’t stand eating a banana with bruises and was glad to see there were none. I peeled another one for my brother. “We don’t have much time,” my dad said, hurrying us out the door.
I looked for a smile from my dad.
Read an interview with the author for the story behind the story.
He had a great smile, a mouth full of even teeth, and a dimple in each cheek. He was wearing his work clothes, not his nice ones. He wore nice clothes no matter the occasion, except when he went to work. None of the wool suits at the shops around here fit him, so he would buy the fabric at a store and take it to the one tailor he knew. That way, the shoulder stitching wouldn’t hang below his shoulder and his pants wouldn’t drag on the ground. You couldn’t tell he was short.
The tailor worked out of his home, not far from where we lived. My dad’s pieces were side projects the tailor took on for extra cash. He worked on them when he had time. There was never a finish date set, and my dad wasn’t pushy about it. My dad wasn’t tall, but he was handsome, especially when he wore his suits. He wore them to weddings, funerals, any kind of party or place with a dance floor. And he loved to dance. With Mom, especially. They were the first ones on the dance floor at a wedding. My dad always made sure that anyone who wanted to dance would have a chance to with him.
Whenever my dad went to drop off fabric at the tailor’s or received a call letting him know that the pieces were finished, we’d go with him, to give Mom a break. We’d wait in the car outside the tailor’s. It wasn’t long. Twenty minutes, maybe. He said, “That man doesn’t like kids.” Even if my father was angry or disagreed with someone, he smiled. Just smiled through it all.
My father worked somewhere that had a lot of cardboard boxes. We had a lot of cardboard around our place. We lived in a basement with two bedrooms. My father taped cardboard to all our windows so that no one could see us from the outside, but that also meant that we couldn’t see out from the inside. Still, he kept the cardboard taped to the windows because, he said, “It’s cheaper than curtains. More privacy, too.” My father also cut out a small square of cardboard for us to put our winter boots on. He said, “This way we won’t ruin the floor in the entryway.” I don’t know why he worried about that. It wasn’t like he owned the place. “Doesn’t matter. What if we move out, and someone else comes to live here? We don’t want them to think we’re pigs,” he said.
My brother and I shared one bedroom. He took the top bunk, and I took the bottom. He was two years younger than me, but that difference wasn’t a big deal. We talked about all our friends at school, and their parents, and our parents. “Did you see her dad? I thought he was her grandfather because he was
sooooo oooold!
” We were proud of how young our parents looked. They were often mistaken for teen-agers at the high school just down the hill from our school. And the guys in sixth grade would say to our mom, “What’s
uuup
, girl? You new here?” She’d smile, and me or my brother would say, “That’s our mom!” They’d apologize and ask, “Why’s she young?”
At night, there was always some noise outside that I couldn’t recognize, and it would take me a while to make up something to explain it away before I could calm down and go to sleep. I was a child who lived in my own mind and scared myself, and had a hard time talking myself out of it. Once, I thought I heard gunshots outside, but it was firecrackers going off. It was the Fourth of July. I thought there was a fire outside when what I was smelling was a car’s exhaust. A woman screaming at night turned out to be the blaring siren of an ambulance. For the longest time, there was this pretty, ethereal sound, as if a fairy were about to appear before me, but the fairy never appeared. I couldn’t sleep. When we walked to school, my brother showed me what it was. “Look, it’s that fairy music you hear,” he said, pointing to a porch with a small wind chime hanging from the ceiling.
Podcast: The Writer’s Voice
Listen to Souvankham Thammavongsa read “Wall Cano.”
My brother was really sensitive and noticed things that I didn’t. “Did you see Ryan at school today? He didn’t have anything to eat, and his mom doesn’t pick him up anymore. It’s a woman, but it’s not his mom. And Miss Stevens got a perm,” he said. “Someone called her Miss Curly in class, and everyone laughed. It must be hard to be a teacher. To go to school for so many years and know all that stuff and then come teach us so we know it, too.”
Our dad said that he never got to go to school like us. In Laos, the war came, and that was it. At least he knew how to read people, he said. “I just poo-poo paa-paa my way around until something makes sense to them. That’s how English works.” He smiled, like someone who was about to be hit but thought he could stop the blow if he shrank into himself and made like he was so tiny he wasn’t worth anything. Our mom didn’t know how to read and would tell us to take our questions to our dad. When she was still living with us, she’d grab the side of her head and tell us it hurt, and then she would go into their bedroom and close the door. Because of the cardboard, our place was always so dark.
When I think about it, other people were always trying to break up our parents. There was the woman on the sixth floor, who often forgot her keys and would press our buzzer to get Dad to go out and open the door for her. She knew that our intercom didn’t work properly and that the superintendent hadn’t come around to fix it. So she’d buzz, and Dad would have to go out there and let her into the building, and they’d talk in the hallway. I don’t know what they talked about, but Dad would come back and Mom would be so angry. He’d do his three smiles for her. He’d start with a smile that made his dimples sink in, then his lips would turn tight, as if he were pretending to smile, and then he’d flash a more relaxed smile where the wrinkles in his forehead didn’t show. He’d say he was ugly and no one wanted him, let alone wanted him enough to steal him away. “What for, to be a pet?”
It wasn’t the same when it came to Mom. Any man Mom talked to, our dad said, was a man trying to steal her. So it was our job to watch out for these men and make sure they didn’t come near our mom. “She’s married,” I would say if a man sat next to her on the bus. Me and my brother would squeeze in between to let him know she had children.
One time, at a park on a hot summer day, an old man came out of nowhere and sat on the blanket with our mother. He had hair the color of my pee, and there were so few hairs on his head I could count them all. I’d never seen him before, and I didn’t know who he was. He was the type of person who called my mom a lotus flower or yelled “Ten dollars! Ten dollars!” at her. People like that were always telling us to go home. I don’t know why. It was just a basement. We didn’t even have a balcony.
I tapped my brother on the shoulder and showed him that I had some stones in my hand, and I turned my chin toward the man with my mom. My brother understood. We crept close and hid behind a tree stump that was half poking out of the ground, and we threw the stones at him. We were nice about it at first, using small ones that mostly hit him on the arm. He laughed and kept on trying to talk to her. After that, we knew we had to do greater damage.
I signalled like a soldier to my brother to try a spot on his face. He said, “I don’t want to. He’s just a man.” I did it myself—picked up some more stones, heavier ones, and threw them. They whizzed by the man’s head. Then I picked up another one, and it hit the man on the mouth. My mom looked at us, and then back at the man, and laughed. The man got up off the blanket and shouted at me, “Fucking kids!” I stared back at him and took my index finger and slid it across my neck like it was a knife. I yelled “Fucking old man!” and stuck out my flat chest. My brother slunk away and hid inside an orange tube slide.
We didn’t tell our dad. He wouldn’t have been able to get past the fact that some man had come to talk to our mother, so I couldn’t even tell him how I’d protected her. Some things you just do and you know you did right. You don’t have to wait for someone to tell you.
I didn’t know what homework was. And since my parents had never gone to school themselves, they never asked me about it. I thought that because we spent all day at school sitting at a desk—working—when I got home my evening was supposed to be like Dad’s. It was supposed to be for rest, for watching television as long as my eyes would stay open. I brought schoolwork home with me, but I just left it in a plastic bag by the door. The science project, though, was a big thing. Our teacher had talked about it since the first day, and we were supposed to work on it all year. I’d forgotten about it after Mom left, and now there were only three weeks until this big show. There would be prizes. I’d never won anything before, and my brother said, “Dad can make something easy. First place, too, I bet,” so I told Dad and we scrambled something together two nights before it was due.
He took a piece of cardboard from the corner of our kitchen window and asked me to cut it into small strips, the size of Popsicle sticks. We needed more sticks, he said. The more cardboard we took from the window, the more light we let in, and the more we let people see us. But once we’d got about a hundred of those sticks he began building something. It looked like a house, but not like the houses here. It was on stilts. He said he’d lived in a house like that before we came here. “Now I’m a refugee,” he said. I didn’t know what a refugee was, and neither did my brother, but I thought that since my dad had said he was one that must mean that we were, too, like the way we carry our last name. Whether we wanted that name or not, it was just there, telling everyone where we came from and that we were related.
The thing my father made was tiny and beautiful and so delicate and tender. If it weren’t for the glue, I was pretty sure the whole thing would have fallen apart real easy. I didn’t want to take it to school and have it on display. It was so obvious that I hadn’t built that thing. This was an adult’s hand at work. All the same, I was proud of my dad and what he’d made, and I wanted everyone to see it.
When I brought my dad’s little house into the classroom and placed it on top of my desk, a crowd formed quickly. Everyone was impressed. There were doubts, even accusations already that I hadn’t made it. I didn’t defend myself. I just stayed quiet. I looked around at the other projects. A bowl of water. If you dropped ice cubes into it and then dropped a thread with a bit of salt in, it would melt the ice and the thread would sink into it. A kid held up a thread, and an ice cube dangled from the end of it. Someone else had made an eyeball. It had labels, explaining what each part was called and how it all worked—what happened when a part got damaged and a person couldn’t see. What it means when we wear glasses. I thought that was interesting. Then, there was this brown thing that looked like a pile of shit. I really did not know what it was. It was gigantic and took up a whole table all by itself. Smoke came out of a hole. When someone poured liquid into that hole, you could hear something rumbling and foaming. It was impressive. The moment I saw that thing, I knew that the competition was over and it would win. By the time school ended for the day, the prizes had been awarded. First, second, third, and honorable mention.
I walked home with the thing my dad had made and left it in the living room. I should have just trashed it, but I didn’t have the heart. I knew it was something you didn’t destroy. So I just brought it home.
When my dad came home from work, he came running toward me, excited, and he asked me what we’d won. He was so certain and confident.
I told him that what he’d made didn’t win anything.
I don’t know why it meant so much to him, but my dad began to cry then. His shoulders dropped, and his arms hung by his side. He looked like he was smiling, but he was crying. Tears wet his whole face, even though his eyes were closed. My brother cried, too. He cries at just about everything, and the sight of my father crying—well, it didn’t matter why. He was done for.
I didn’t know what to do for my father then. It didn’t seem right to tell him that things would be fine. It didn’t seem right to tell him there was always next year. It was just that he’d never been to school. He didn’t know you could work so hard and no matter what you did, it wouldn’t be good enough. He didn’t know that once you began to understand something, something else would come along and you’d have to learn to understand it all over again.
He turned to me after he was done crying, wiping his nose and tears. Who won? he asked. He wanted to know. I told him that I couldn’t remember. And it really didn’t matter. What mattered were the hours he’d put into making his house. Making something beautiful that no one had ever seen before. And I don’t know why I said this or where it came from or what I meant exactly, but I said, “Sometimes the winner doesn’t win.”
I didn’t want my father to know that something called a “wall cano” that looked like a pile of shit with foam coming out of its hole had won first place. Or that an eyeball thing had won second. Or that a stupid trick with ice cubes had won third. I just knew not to bring my schoolwork home and have my dad help me ever again for as long as I lived. I would go it alone. The man just wasn’t cut out for that stuff.
Not long after this, I thought I saw my mom across the street from my school. I felt something bright draw my eyes, and when I looked a woman was standing there, but I wasn’t sure if it was her. She had messy hair, and her clothes looked too big. I told my dad that night. He smiled at me without showing any of his teeth and pretended that I hadn’t said anything, and told me to finish my dinner. I tried to talk to my brother about it when we were alone in our room. I thought maybe he could tell me if it was her, and we’d talk about where she was or might be. But he also got quiet, tried a few words, and then disappeared into the dark. He pretended that I hadn’t said anything, too. People become who they are, and I think that’s a moment when my brother became who he is now.
I am not ten years old anymore, but I still have the same feelings at thirty-seven. Once, I was visiting a friend when she put up a finger like she’d heard a sound from the ceiling, but that was her way of telling me to pause our conversation. She leaned back in her chair and called out to her ten-year-old to remind him about his book report. He said he’d done it already, and he brought the report over for her to read, to look for spelling mistakes, to check for clarity. She reminded him what to aim for. A clear beginning, a middle, and an end. My friend had gone all the way in school. She’d finished and taken all the degrees. When I was ten, I did not have her, someone like her. I had to learn all that by myself. Out of order, probably. Middle, beginning, end. End, beginning, middle. End. What is an end, and when you think you have one, where does it go, exactly, when there is no one to tell you? ♦
By Cressida Leyshon

Books
The Gold Rush and the Making of Modern America
The best-selling author Nathaniel Philbrick sees links between eighteen-fifties California and the current A.I. boom. What can the history of the action-packed gold rush actually tell us?
By
Kathryn Schulz
Sam Pit, a Native American who worked at Sutter’s Mill. Countless Indigenous people were killed during the gold rush.Photograph courtesy the California History Room / California State Library
Eight pages into “
The Rush: California Gold, the Civil War, and the Making of the Modern World
” (Viking), Nathaniel Philbrick tells us why he wrote it. Philbrick, who is seventy years old, has lived for the past four decades on Nantucket, a home that has doubled as the wellspring of his career. After publishing two books about its history—“
Away Off Shore: Nantucket Island and Its People, 1602-1890
” and “
Abram’s Eyes: The Native American Legacy of Nantucket Island
”—he turned his attention to one of the countless whaling ships that sailed forth from the island in the nineteenth century. This was the Essex, which weighed anchor there in 1819 and was subsequently destroyed by a sperm whale in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, stranding its steadily dwindling number of crew members at sea for three horror-filled months and inspiring Herman Melville’s “
Moby-Dick
.”
Philbrick’s own gripping narrative of the fate of the Essex, “In the Heart of the Sea,” marked a turning point in his career. It won a National Book Award, in 2000, spent forty weeks on the New York
Times
best-seller list, was adapted into a Hollywood movie, and made its author an eminence in the field of Dad History. Philbrick’s subsequent books include popular-in-both-senses accounts of the Mayflower, the Battle of Bunker Hill, and the Battle of Yorktown. With one exception, a book about the Battle of the Little Bighorn, they have been set on the East Coast or on the ocean or both, natural enough contexts for a man who has spent most of his life on an island off the coast of New England.

So why California all of a sudden? Because, Philbrick tells us, so many Nantucketers before him developed an abrupt interest in it, too. After gold was discovered in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada, men who were born and raised to make their living from the sea sailed their whaleships fourteen thousand miles to San Francisco, abandoned them in the harbor, and rushed inland to try to make their living from the ground instead. “Over the course of nine months in 1849,” Philbrick writes, “Nantucket, once the whaling capital of the world, lost a quarter of its voting population to the goldfields.” That is a staggering fact, one that drags behind it a whole ghost book about what happened to Nantucket and countless other places across the country after so many of their citizens left to try to strike it rich in California.
This is not Philbrick’s subject, but almost everything else is. “The Rush” is a sprawling book, characters and stories spilling out everywhere, as dense with claims as the goldfields it describes. Of these, two emerge as dominant. The first, which is woven throughout the book—albeit in the strict sense that it keeps appearing and disappearing—is that the discovery of gold in California set off a mad scramble for wealth, land, labor, and power that contributed to the onset of the Civil War and then helped determine its outcome. The second is that what mattered most about the gold rush was not the gold but the rush. The headlong haste with which those Nantucket whalers picked up their lives and went West was representative, Philbrick argues, of a new and distinctly American appetite for speed, novelty, and transformation, one that has defined our character and shaped our future from the time of the forty-niners to the planned Anthropic I.P.O.
“Somebody needs to tell him we can all do that.”
Cartoon by Will Kiley Santino
“The Rush” is not particularly convincing about either of these claims. This is partly because both are a little rickety and partly because they are too different to comfortably coexist in a single book: one is about history and causality, the other is about psychology and culture. Mostly, though, it is because Philbrick keeps veering off into a larger, messier, less instrumentalized account of the gold rush and its aftermath. A better title for his book would be “A History of California, 1848-1878.” Lest that strike you as dull, consider that those are three of the most thrilling, harrowing, and action-packed decades since the founding of our nation. In a sense, then, the tacit question “The Rush” asks is not about the history it covers but about history in general: Does the past need to explain the present to be worthy of our attention?
If you know anything at all about the gold rush, you’ve likely heard the story of Sutter’s Mill, whose construction on the banks of the American River unearthed the shining flecks that, in January, 1848, kicked off the whole adventure. Philbrick, who understands that what happened next had less to do with good luck than with force, influence, and cunning, swiftly turns away from John Sutter, who never got rich off the wealth beneath his mill, to introduce a man named Samuel Brannan. At the time, Brannan was the leader of San Francisco’s Mormon community, though no one who subsequently knew him would have called him godly. When he heard about the discovery at Sutter’s Mill, he did not head toward the mountains. Instead, he bought up every pick and shovel he could lay his hands on, then paraded through town waving around gold dust and telling anyone who would listen where to find it. In short order, Philbrick writes, San Francisco was half empty and “Brannan was on his way to becoming a millionaire.” When Brigham Young caught wind of all this and asked his West Coast emissary to remit the appropriate tithe, Brannan supposedly told him to have God send the receipt. That was the end of his stint as a Mormon.
News of the gold spread fast, not least because people kept discovering more of it. In most places on Earth, gold is sparsely distributed, averaging around five parts per billion. But, in the California Mother Lode, a hundred-and-fifty-mile stretch of the Sierra Nevada, you could find it almost everywhere: in extant streams and ancient riverbeds, in gravel bars and veins of quartz, in sand and soil and silt and sometimes, on a very good day, just sitting there. By the end of 1848, it seemed that half the nation was dreaming of going West to claim a share of it. But there was a problem: the available steamboat and railroad routes terminated at the Missouri River, two thousand miles from the California goldfields. To get there by land, you had to traverse, by foot and wagon, the Great Plains, the Rocky Mountains, the deserts and salt flats—whose fatal aridity was soon evidenced by the discarded belongings and bleaching bones of earlier parties—and, finally, the sheer walls of the Sierras, which, no matter how exhausted and emaciated both man and beast were by then, had to be crossed before the snow started falling. All told, the journey generally took half a year. Nearly one in ten did not survive it.
The wonder is how many attempted it. In 1849 alone, more than forty thousand people travelled overland to California, while roughly the same number headed there by sea. This sometimes entailed sailing to Panama, crossing the jungled isthmus partly by canoe and partly by foot, horse, or mule, then waiting for another vessel on the Pacific side—a shorter journey, in theory, if the bottleneck wasn’t too bad and you didn’t succumb to malaria or yellow fever. Alternatively, you could do what those Nantucketers had done and set sail from the East Coast, track southward all the way to Cape Horn, pass through the terrifying waters where the world’s two largest oceans meet, then head north again, clear around the hemisphere to San Francisco. That, too, took around six months, plus an iron stomach.
No matter the route, the duration of the journey was at drastic odds with its perceived urgency. Those who were obsessed with reaching the goldfields were maddened by the exigencies of getting there, and so, Philbrick writes, “a seething impatience gripped the American people that hasn’t let go of us yet.” What drove these California-bound migrants particularly crazy, he continues, was “the knowledge that tens of thousands of people are
already there.
” Some of these were long-standing residents; Native Americans had called the region home for millennia, and, in 1849, tens of thousands of them lived in the vicinity of the Mother Lode. So did many Mexicans, known as Californios, who had lately been expatriated without moving an inch: California had been part of Mexico until 1848, when it was ceded to the United States at the end of the Mexican-American War.
But others were recent arrivals. Even Australians who wanted to get to San Francisco had less than half as far to travel as someone sailing from New York, and more than ten thousand of them soon passed through the Golden Gate. China was likewise comparatively proximate, and huge numbers of its people crossed the Pacific to reach the mines. Immigrants poured in from Latin America, too, especially Chileans, who hailed from a country rich in precious metals, and who taught many a New England lawyer and Midwestern farm boy the art of mining. Thirty thousand French people came to seek their fortunes as well; locals called them Keskadees, a corruption of “Qu’est-ce qu’il a dit?”—what did he say?
Well might they ask. The newly named city of San Francisco, which had been a sleepy port village with perhaps eight hundred residents in 1848, suddenly became a booming Tower of Babel. By 1849, property there had become some of the most expensive in the nation, even when it wasn’t desirable, or, for that matter, habitable; many people lived in tents, but there was also a thriving business in “water lots,” which were staked out in the bay to someday be filled with rubble and converted to land. The streets, where they existed, were tunnels of wind-whipped dust in the dry season—one resident called it Sand Francisco—and a muddy mess the rest of the year. Out in the harbor, the skeletons of derelict ships abandoned by sailors who had gone searching for gold formed the first and strangest San Francisco skyline. And yet this inhospitable, half-built, helter-skelter city was, for a while, the destination of choice for profiteers, speculators, and schemers from every corner of the globe.
While California was becoming a magnet for those from abroad, it was provoking a political crisis at home. In 1849, there were thirty united states—fifteen of them slaveholding, fifteen of them free. Constantly rebalancing that map had been an unhappy necessity from the earliest days of the Republic, but the discovery of gold in the brand-new territory of California set off a national furor over what kind of state it would be.
Most histories of the Civil War divide the nation into North and South. Give or take Bleeding Kansas, most also focus their attention east of the Mississippi River. “The Rush” redraws that map, relocating the center of gravity westward, to California. As Philbrick makes clear, sectarian concerns over who would control the state’s wealth ran high from the beginning, and many of those who went West after 1848 were not just seeking a private fortune. Instead, as would later happen in Kansas and Nebraska, slaveowners and Southern sympathizers on the one hand and abolitionists and Free-Soilers on the other all flocked to California to try to tip the political scales in their favor.
In this demographic competition, the South had both geography and weather on its side. Migrants from the slave states could head West at any time of the year, along a route known as the Gila Trail, which passed through New Mexico and Arizona to the southern edge of California. By contrast, those from the Northern states had to time their journeys carefully, since the Rockies and the Sierras could not be crossed in winter. In part because of this advantage, the South made steady inroads in the California interior, where town after town soon announced its cultural allegiance right on Main Street, via businesses like the Texas Saloon, the Mississippi Shoe Shop, and the Alabama Emporium.
Still, the North quickly established a strong presence in San Francisco, and it had something going for it in the goldfields, too: thanks to their work, many miners had a profound antipathy to forced labor. Philbrick tells the story of a Texan who showed up in a popular mining area and started staking claims not only for himself but also for his fifteen enslaved workers; in short order, he was run out by outraged locals. This resistance to slavery had little or nothing to do with humane fellow-feeling. “Not one in ten cares a button for its abolition,” the then mayor of Monterey wrote, of the miners there. The real issue was that the presence of the enslaved in the gold mines increased the ranks of the competition.
In the end, of course, the opponents of slavery were victorious. When a group of delegates assembled to write a constitution for California, in the autumn of 1849, they unanimously agreed that, within its borders, “neither slavery, nor involuntary servitude, unless for the punishment of crimes, shall ever be tolerated.” A year later, via the Compromise of 1850, California officially became the Union’s thirty-first state and its sixteenth free one. But this triumph came at a considerable cost to the rest of the nation: in exchange, the South got a dramatically harsher Fugitive Slave Act, which stipulated that all American citizens could be required to help capture runaway slaves, and established heavy fines and prison sentences for those who aided fugitives.
Meanwhile, trouble was also brewing in California, where surface gold was getting harder to find and the competition for it was getting uglier. Gangs of armed Americans fanned local resentment of immigrants and steadily drove them off their claims and out of the country. A new law required Californios to prove the validity of their property titles in court, an expensive process that took an average of seventeen years; meanwhile, squatters made use of extrajudicial means, from burning crops to outright murder, to make them give up their increasingly valuable land. But the worst fate befell the region’s Native Americans, who were first driven from the goldfields and then subjected to a campaign of wholesale annihilation. White militias destroyed their homes, torched their food supplies, and slaughtered them outright so routinely that a secondary economy of kidnappers sprang up to sell the survivors, children and adults alike, into servitude.
Philbrick relates all this less as history than as a stage play. He is fond of characters and good at depicting them, and he does not so much trace the influence of the gold rush on the Civil War as introduce us to various people with a stake in its outcome. One of these was William Gwin, a wealthy Mississippi plantation owner turned California power broker who was bent on aligning his new home with the slave states and making himself one of its first senators. Another was David Broderick, a working-class Irish American politician from New York whose crew of henchmen belied his sensitive streak; he didn’t drink, never married, avoided brothels, spent his free time alone reading literature, and despised the institution of slavery.
Both Gwin and Broderick ultimately ended up in the Senate, and Philbrick describes the clash between them as “the center of the narrative” of his book. But that is not the reader’s experience, partly because “The Rush” is too desultory to have a center and partly because neither man stands out particularly clearly against the ensemble cast. This includes at least thirty-three major characters, some of whom are more memorable than the putative protagonists. The abolitionist Jessie Frémont, for instance, was married to the famous war hero John Frémont but was, as a contemporary observer commented, “the better man of the two.” After John lost the 1856 Presidential election to James Buchanan, it was widely whispered, according to her obituary, “that if the lovely Jessie had been the actual candidate, she, and not Buchanan, would have occupied the Presidential chair.”
Another star turn goes to Mary Ellen Pleasant, who was arguably America’s first Black millionaire and inarguably one of the most canny and chameleonlike figures this country has ever produced. “I am a whole theatre unto myself,” she once declared, and it was true; she was, among many other things, an abolitionist, a civil-rights activist, a domestic worker, a domineering owner of boarding houses and laundries, and a supporter of John Brown, though Philbrick gives far too much credence to her claim to have been his most important financial backer.
It is a pleasure to meet these people in “The Rush,” but not every character makes an equally strong case for belonging there. Primary sources are a necessary and wonderful tool for historians, but they can have a fun-house-mirror effect, making some aspects of the past bulge and others narrow. To his credit, Philbrick is sensitive to those parts which we usually see inaccurately or not at all. He tells us, for example, that, although more than ten thousand Chinese workers helped build the transcontinental railroad, not a single diary or letter from one of them has ever been found, leaving a vast lacuna where their own California story should be.
Still, “The Rush” is ultimately more hamstrung by what it contains than by what it does not. We spend the first fifty pages of it following one Vicente Rosales, a Chilean man who arrived in California in early 1849. Rosales was a keen observer of life in and around the goldfields, but his experiences there, though interesting, don’t really bear on any of Philbrick’s broader themes. Yet we are spared no detail about him—down to the number of cows he brought home from a visit to Monterey and the day job of the man who once dug a well for him—and one suspects that Rosales earned his lengthy place in these pages not because his story was particularly relevant but because he documented it so thoroughly.
A similar problem of abundance attends the book over all. Philbrick has a keen eye and a magpie curiosity, and he can’t stop finding fascinating tidbits to share, from the 1850 flooding of the city of Sacramento to a brawl on the floor of the House that made thirty-seven members of Congress, many of them otherwise given to bloviating, forget the old dictum about using your words. All this is fun to read, since Philbrick is an adept and congenial storyteller. But well told is not the same as telling, and, in the end, the overarching claims in his book are occluded rather than revealed by the surfeit of detail.
Or perhaps the claims themselves are the problem. It is true, of course, that the discovery of gold in California altered the balance of the states and the economics of the nation, but Philbrick never mounts a convincing case that it was therefore decisive to the course and conclusion of the Civil War. Yes, the Compromise of 1850 played a role, but so did a series of political and constitutional crises that had little or nothing to do with California and its gold, including the Missouri Compromise, the Kansas-Nebraska Act, the Dred Scott decision, and the election of Abraham Lincoln. To support the claim that California’s enormous wealth helped win the war, Philbrick quotes Ulysses S. Grant saying, while the battles were still raging, that he did not know what the North would do “if it were not for the gold sent from California.” That’s interesting but hardly probative, and countless other factors, unmentioned by Philbrick, contributed to the stronger financial position of the North, such as greater banking and borrowing power and a more industrialized economy and a larger population.
Philbrick himself, having set out to write about the gold rush and the Civil War, nonetheless seems tentative about the relationship between the two, and the one he establishes is not so much causal as metaphorical. “The discovery of gold in California,” he writes, “was part of a much larger—and ultimately more consequential—rush: the rush to the Civil War.” Yet even the metaphor stumbles, since it is hard to see anything like the mad frenzy of the forty-niners in the very long road to the Civil War, whose origins date all the way back to the founding of the United States.
How much explanatory work can—or should—a single word do? From the title on down, “The Rush” makes much of the idea of rushing, of the allure and danger of speed and impulsivity. Indeed, that idea becomes the book’s organizing principle; it explains why we skip over most of the Civil War itself, which cannot be contained within that rubric, but spend fifty pages on the construction of the transcontinental railroad, a way to hasten the movement of people and capital across the country. And it explains, too, the otherwise odd finale of “The Rush,” which concerns the photographer Eadweard Muybridge. In 1860, Muybridge was thrown from a carriage, resulting in a head injury that radically changed his personality and possibly heightened his artistic inclinations. The accident took place in what is now southeast Oklahoma, and Muybridge, headed for Europe, was planning to put a whole ocean between himself and the goldfields, yet Philbrick writes that “Muybridge had been brain-damaged by the Rush.”
That strains credulity, but the larger question is what Muybridge is doing in this book in the first place, other than famously taking mid-gallop pictures of a horse belonging to Leland Stanford—the former governor of California and the owner of a sprawling estate south of San Francisco that he named for an exceptionally tall redwood tree nearby. The answer is that Muybridge helps form the dots Philbrick wants to connect for us by way of conclusion: the invention of motion pictures (“the Rush could now be projected onto a screen through a gas-lit device Muybridge called the Zoopraxiscope”), the origins of Palo Alto (meaning “tall tree”), and the founding of Stanford University, “the nucleus of what we now call Silicon Valley,” which “spawned one technological ‘gold rush’ after another—the microprocessor, the microcomputer, the internet, and artificial intelligence.” Like so many of us, Philbrick is gravely worried about the latter: “We are all passengers on a hurtling train. The end of humanity might be the ultimate destination.”
In Philbrick’s framing, the root cause of this crisis was the discovery of gold in California nearly two centuries ago. “This is the world in which we live today,” he writes earlier in the book, “jammed into jets on our frantic way to the next new thing—a world created in 1849 by the California Gold Rush.” But did the gold rush create our contemporary world, or do the two just resemble each other? It’s true that many features of eighteen-fifties California are also visible in the current A.I. boom, from the benefits of arriving early and the outlandish profit to be made in infrastructure—whether picks and shovels or microchips and data centers—to political instability, environmental destruction, and wild inequality. But resemblance is just a surface relationship, and nothing in Philbrick’s book makes the gold rush seem like a motive force behind the breakneck, and maybe break-everything, boom of today. Nor does anything in it make avaricious urgency seem specifically American; how could it be, when all those Aussies and Frenchmen and Chinese and Chileans likewise dropped everything and sped to California?
The more plausible explanation is this: put any group of people within striking distance of a potential source of spectacular wealth, and many of them will behave in similar ways, including moving toward it, competing for it, cheating over it, exaggerating about it, inventing new ways to extract it, creating rules to manage access to it, breaking those rules, and generally using all available means, legal and otherwise, to dominate and profit from it. “The Rush” is at its best when it simply shows us this mayhem as it unfolded in a specific place and period, instigated, abetted, opposed, documented, and occasionally averted by marvellously specific human beings. One sympathizes, in these dark and confusing times, with the desire for the past to illuminate the present. But the past is its own kind of gold—abundant, difficult to access, inordinately valuable—and sometimes it is enough to let it shine. ♦

Ausländer
, by Michael Moritz (Pegasus)
. This piercing family memoir assembles a portrait of a clan that, like millions of others, was “torn to shreds by the most murderous whirlwind of the twentieth century”: the Holocaust. Moritz, a successful venture capitalist, summons up his relatives vividly. Among them is his paternal grandfather, Max Moritz, who fought for Germany in the First World War, only to be later murdered by Nazis at Dachau. Michael was born in Wales—his father, Alfred, came to England as a teen-ager, and his mother, Doris Rath, arrived on the Kindertransport—and his account is filled with both historical detail and candid observations about the gap between his and his parents’ experiences, and about his mother’s and father’s respective attitudes toward their lost homeland.
Frivolity: A Defense
, by Jehanne Dubrow (Columbia)
. This roving work mounts an investigation into that which is typically dismissed as unserious—for example, fashion, perfume, and romantic comedies. Dubrow argues that the charge of frivolity often serves to disparage figures and activities associated with femininity and queerness, by tying those qualities to vanity and indulgence, and she attempts to make a case for its necessity. “Frivolity calls us to our bodies,” she writes, “which crave pleasure and joy.” Though the connections that Dubrow draws between subjects can sometimes feel forced, she nevertheless offers a thought-provoking meander through a charming array of artifacts and ideas.

May We Feed the King
, by Rebecca Perry (Transit)
. This poetic début novel, a finalist for the Booker Prize, is narrated largely by an unnamed curator who specializes in reconstructing scenes from the past. Her “guiding rule” is to make viewers feel as if those who would’ve inhabited her installations “have just left the room.” At the story’s outset, she begins a commission at a medieval palace, and decides to re-create a room that would have housed a particular king, whose reign has been reduced to just a single page in the historical record. Soon, the curator is transported into that king’s world, but it remains unclear whether the narrative that unfolds is a figment of her imagination. Such is the novel’s own guiding rule, to refute “the idea that we owe anyone the answers they seek—for they are theirs alone to find.”
Sophie, Standing There
,
by Meg Mason (HarperCollins)
. The protagonist of this engrossing novel, Sophie, begins the story freshly separated, broke, and working on the production crew of a local literary festival. Her existence is relatively isolated—she is estranged from her best friend, and confides only in her brother—until she becomes obsessed with a writer named Lilac Dunne. Sophie, along with reading Dunne’s books, listens constantly to podcasts on which she appears, and even speaks to an invented version of her, as though she were a friend. When Dunne comes to the festival and the two meet in real life, the author is icy—but also seems interested in Sophie, much to Sophie’s surprise. As their relationship develops, the roots of Sophie’s isolation are revealed—a turn that charges the novel’s argument for the value of connection, literary and personal.

Why the Broadway Musical Refuses to Die
Broadway once thrived on the collision of musical traditions. Now, amid jukebox shows and Hollywood adaptations, can it recover its creative daring?
By
Adam Gopnik
Great American ballads tend to be theatrically inert: singers like Bob Dylan and Joni Mitchell often reflect on experience in the form of a private soliloquy, while theatrical songs need to give a character something to do—persuade someone, resist someone, make a decision.Illustration by Ximo Abadía
The Broadway musical astonishes us by its continued existence. Thrown off balance first by the talkies, then by television—not to mention the pop-music revolution of the sixties, which quickly made its narrative style (set, scene, song, repeat) seem dated—it should surely have died a quiet death many years ago. Some outdated genres really do die: those paintings of bank C.E.O.s or college presidents lining executive conference rooms seemed formidable until the postwar era, when they began to look wan and embarrassing and make you wish for a photograph.
Yet the Broadway musical persists, in its wholly impossible format, imposing eight big singing shows a week on its stars, which is, as any veteran will tell you, one of the most brutal workloads possible for a performer—and, when it occurs in long-running shows, mostly invisible as a personal triumph. The Phantom in the thirtieth year of “The Phantom of the Opera” might just as well be a phantom. For all that, theatre after theatre fills, leaving new shows searching for a landing spot. Much of this is the simple economics of New York tourism, but some significant part of the persistence stems from the genuine devotion to an otherwise dated craft by an ardent niche audience—akin to the wine world, another diversion that ought to have been fully mechanized long ago but never quite has been. A subgroup of obsessives keeps the quality alive through sheer passion.
