What perpetual-motion engine does the musical run on? In search of a partial answer, the conductor John Mauceri and the Columbia linguist John H. McWhorter have now collaborated on a new and amiably revisionist history, “
Broadway in Black and White: The Untold Story of the American Musical
” (Norton). Focussed on an interchange that may seem, from a conventional point of view, auxiliary but is in fact foundational, their book’s “untold story” is that of the Black Broadway musical and of how its reception, sometimes hot and sometimes cold, shaped more familiar stories and shows. The book moves from the still minstrelsy-adjacent productions of the twenties—“Shuffle Along,” “Blackbirds”—through various appropriations of the style by such landmark musicals as “Show Boat” and “Porgy and Bess,” to much later shows like “The Wiz,” the Black adaptation of “The Wizard of Oz,” which was a huge hit in its day. All of this leads inevitably to “Hamilton,” that most improbable apotheosis in the history of entertainment, in which a show essentially about quarrels over the federal government’s debt-assumption policy in the late eighteenth century became, for a while, a felt vehicle for American racial redemption. What emerges is that part of the musical’s staying power rises from its capacity to meld musical traditions, and make that marriage embody the political preoccupations of changing times.
Our two authors collaborate, unusually, by addressing the reader in alternation, with Mauceri’s musical knowledge balancing McWhorter’s broader social nous, sometimes with a lovely idiosyncrasy: Mauceri points out that a man named McWhorter criticized “South Pacific” for its preachiness, and McWhorter adds that the critic may have been related to the family who once owned his ancestors. Together, they make a persuasive case that the signature style of the Broadway musical was the genius of Black agony passed through the prism of Jewish melancholy. It probably isn’t insignificant that the creators of such classics as “West Side Story” and “Hello, Dolly!” were all gay Jewish men. Broadway’s affinity for certain kinds of outsiders helps explain something about its style: its makers struggled to slip “subversive” material into their shows while struggling just as hard never to seem subversive. Their art drew energy from the tension between those impulses. (Mauceri and McWhorter belong to the small fringe group of heterosexual non-Jews who live a furtive, shadowy existence within the Broadway world, knowing their own kind at a glance yet never fully accepted by the mainstream.)
Though the specifically Black shows were marginalized, the effect of their music—amplified, of course, through the larger megaphone of jazz recordings—was seminal. One has only to compare Jerome Kern’s beautiful but still Viennese-inflected scores for the “Princess” musicals he wrote with P. G. Wodehouse in the nineteen-tens to any Gershwin score of the twenties to sense how large a change this was, as Black sounds entered the theatre and never left.
Yet one language can have many dialects within it. What is striking about the “crossover” music that Mauceri and McWhorter examine is that, in Black blues-based Broadway songs, the minor thirds and bent notes tend to carry the more sombre meaning of the words, whereas in their Great White Way versions they are more purely romantic, registering an emotional high, not a low. In Fats Waller’s “What Did I Do to Be So Black and Blue?”—written for the 1929 Broadway musical “Hot Chocolates”—the blue notes and expressive wail land tellingly on the words “black and blue” in the lyric. In a great blues-derived ballad like the Gershwins’ “How Long Has This Been Going On?,” written for the original “Funny Face” just a couple of years earlier, the blue note lands on the “going on?” query of the title. (The singer is comparing kisses sold at a charity fair to the real thing.) The same musical inflection that voices humiliation in Waller’s song becomes an expression of delighted discovery in the Gershwins’. The white composers took a demotic, street-made style and turned it into one that was declamatory and stage-bound.
The music of the Broadway musical has several lives, or layers. Blues and ragtime supplied a largely Black musical language that helped American composers break free of European operetta, even as jazz performers then gave them a life beyond the theatre. Cole Porter’s songs of the thirties, for instance, are better known through Frank Sinatra’s recordings of the fifties than through earlier theatrical recordings, while Ella Fitzgerald’s songbook series offers an encyclopedic survey of the Broadway repertory, particularly the songs of Gershwin, Berlin, and Rodgers. Just as we are told to love the sinner and hate the sin, it has been possible in the past to love the songs and hate the singers, or at least the scenes and scenery in which the songs were originally set. Wilfrid Sheed’s fine volume on the American songbook, “The House That George Built,” treats the shows themselves with indifference and sometimes embarrassment. A caustic critic of Sheed’s generation could recoil from the sentimentality of “Oklahoma!” or even “Carousel” while loving Fitzgerald’s or Sinatra’s versions of the songs they contain. Broadway had adapted Black musical forms to the demands of theatrical storytelling; jazz performers took the resulting songs back out of their theatrical settings and made them their own.
The most arresting chapters in Mauceri and McWhorter’s book are devoted to “Porgy and Bess,” the Gershwins’ 1935 “folk opera.” The authors aren’t much interested in condemning it, the way some do, as opportunistic cultural appropriation, with Broadway composers appointing themselves spokespeople for the Black residents of Catfish Row (which it is), or saluting it as an enduring American classic (which it also is). From the outset, they point out, “Porgy” gave Black performers a rare opportunity to play major, fully human roles in New York’s commercial theatre, without a hint of Tomming. Eighty years before “Hamilton,” the Gershwins contractually reserved the Black roles for Black performers, a condition that persists today.
Mauceri and McWhorter also trace the appreciation of the show, and the novel it was based on, among Harlem Renaissance figures, who saw empathy in what others saw as condescension. Even Maya Angelou recalled that her first encounter with the piece left her “totally consumed,” even “stunned,” because it “had shown me the greatest array of Negro talent I had ever seen.” She went on to win a dancing role in the touring company. McWhorter writes that his mother was “typical of her Black generation” in adoring “Porgy and Bess”: “What mattered was that Black characters were singing some of the most beautiful music ever written.” DuBose Heyward’s novel is, in fact, anything but condescending to its characters, and it is frank about their mistrust of even well-meaning whites like its author. Mauceri and McWhorter show how “Porgy and Bess” gives its Black characters an unusual sense of roundness: Bess’s “romance” with Crown is a grownup erotic addiction that the decent, disabled Porgy cannot rival, one that’s fuelled by a parallel addiction to cocaine. (It’s easy to forget that the lovable Sportin’ Life is a drug dealer.)
George Gershwin conceived the work as an opera, drawing on a stage adaptation by Heyward and his wife, Dorothy, but it arrived in New York on Broadway, playing eight times a week at what is now the Neil Simon Theatre. However ambitious, it was crafted as a musical. The more self-consciously operatic versions aren’t necessarily closer to the composer’s intentions. Often overlooked, too, is the blending of DuBose Heyward’s solemn lyrics with Ira Gershwin’s Upper West Side wit: Ira wrote “It Ain’t Necessarily So,” DuBose wrote “Summertime,” and they collaborated on “Bess You Is My Woman Now.” Lyrics are notoriously hard to collaborate on; here, mutual respect met a division of labor, one wry, one wise.
Cartoon by Bruno Pieroni
One comes away from the book thinking of “Porgy and Bess” as perhaps the greatest triumph of Broadway sensibility: Black musical traditions reimagined through the Gershwins’ show-business genius and the Heywards’ storytelling, then deepened by Black jazz performers. McWhorter observes that in “Bess You Is My Woman Now” the blue note falls on the first syllable of “woman,” where it “seemed to suggest sexual attraction.” And, yes, the best versions of the songs may be those that spring free of the opera, including Ella Fitzgerald and Louis Armstrong’s deeply personal account and a later one by Ray Charles and Cleo Laine. American music’s endless spiralling outward is nowhere clearer than in the afterlives of “I Loves You, Porgy.” Black style passes through Gershwin and out into Nina Simone’s famous take and Bill Evans’s imperishable version, where the blues is filtered through Erik Satie’s minimalism to become a haunted, achingly beautiful elegy. Of such social spirals great music is made.
“Broadway in Black and White” feels generally revivifying in its insistence on taking the musical seriously. Yet the obsessive reader may come away feeling a little discouraged, because the world it describes had an organic dynamism that seems hard to retrieve. Of course, every form feels in crisis or exhausted to its admirers at any moment—if the musical is in trouble, it should look over its shoulder at its cousin, the straight problem play, which is surely in even worse shape. Still, it sometimes seems as if three kinds of weeds—the jukebox show, the campy meta-parody show, and the I.P. show—have been outcompeting the native flowers on Forty-second Street.
The jukebox shows (“MJ,” “Jersey Boys,” “Beautiful: The Carole King Musical”) are fun if you already like the music, mostly dispiriting if you want to hear something new. The meta-musicals have their delights but can be no less demoralizing. “The Book of Mormon” and “Spamalot” are the best loved and most efficiently funny examples; the recently revived “Gutenberg! The Musical!” is the most mechanical. But Mel Brooks’s lovable “The Producers” also qualifies as one, with a make-believe score, scavenged from other people’s clichés, that relentlessly and affectionately sends up the musical’s hard-won conventions. The scores and scenes of these productions offer the safety of all meta-art: Are we kidding or not? Who cares! The musical’s storytelling tropes have become so familiar that parody can deliver the very pleasures it mocks, even as the labor of love that established its conventions gets lost in the joke. The I.P. shows, based on some recognizable “property”—“The Outsiders” or “Water for Elephants” or “Death Becomes Her”—usually end up feeling less realized than executed. (“The Outsiders” won the Tony for Best Musical, and certainly worked onstage, but I have never met anyone who can summon up a single song from the show.)
A familiar movie can acquire a richer musical life, as “Big Fish” and “The Band’s Visit” demonstrate. These shows, along with other notable musicals of this century, such as “The Light in the Piazza,” are among those inspired by Stephen Sondheim’s imposing example. Sondheim’s influence in his world—only the influence of Balanchine in American ballet is comparable—is such that, already the subject of a few biographies, he is now the subject of yet another, Daniel Okrent’s “
Stephen Sondheim: Art Isn’t Easy
,” part of Yale University Press’s Jewish Lives series. And a good one it is. We are reminded that Sondheim was not merely a dramatist but a self-dramatizer: he often referred to a letter that his mother wrote him saying that she wished he’d never been born, but the letter may have been fabricated or misrepresented by the son, to organize his own feelings of abandonment while assigning blame to Mom.
A great example, of course, can be a roadblock as much as a path forward. Sondheim’s implicit possibilities were broad; his explicit rules were narrow, emphasizing scene and storytelling at the expense of the delight in wit and melody that had long distinguished American songs from those of European operetta. (Like every artist, Sondheim made his best work at right angles to his professed beliefs: so many of his best songs are either exercises in linguistic play for its own sake, like “Uptown, Downtown,” or stand-alone soliloquies rising from the artist’s isolated heart.) But Sondheim is a jealous God, or at least his acolytes are even more easily enraged than acolytes usually are. As a Sondheim schismatic myself, worshipping and wondering at the same time, I have found what generations of heretics have found: you can protest the purity of your faith as loudly as you like while they drag you to the scaffold.
The Sondheim scruples, Okrent shows, begin with what he overlearned from Oscar Hammerstein, his beloved mentor: the priority of storytelling over the sensual delight of wordplay—a decent rule for beginners, but not one that Shakespeare ever followed—and the greeting-card habit of moralized instruction. Sondheim’s worst songs are dragged down by uplift, whose insincerity shines right through. The man who wrote “Finishing the Hat,” about the artist’s essential and incurable solitude, did not for a moment believe that “No One Is Alone,” as the hastily written eleven-o’clock number of “Into the Woods” would have it. He thought that we are all alone pretty much all the time, amid small, intense, providential pacts of togetherness. “Sunday” is about the accidental urban coexistence that cities provide and artists perceive, rather than “community” or common experience. For all his insistence on making the song match the scene, to the straitjacketing detriment of some of his students, he, like all real artists, wrote one song over and over: the tale of a lonely artist desperately seeking to connect.
For decades, a hope has persisted: that the popular music of the rock era and beyond, the “second American songbook,” would invigorate the Broadway tradition. There have been high-profile breakthroughs, like “Hair” and “Tommy” and “Jesus Christ Superstar,” but they remain isolated monuments rather than the foundation of a form. Even ventures involving songwriters of genius, including Paul Simon’s “The Capeman” and the Bob Dylan-inspired “Girl from the North Country,” have often felt oddly flightless. The attraction is obvious; the difficulty lies in what the songs are built for. A theatrical song gives a character something to do: persuade someone, resist someone, make a decision. The great modern American ballad, from Dylan or Joni Mitchell or Simon, often takes the form of a private self-inspection, a singer reflecting on experience. Even when songs like “Bridge Over Troubled Water” or “A Case of You” address another person, their emotional drama unfolds within the singer’s own soul. Such songs can illuminate a character’s feelings while leaving the scene where it was. Poetically alight, they are theatrically inert. (Billy Joel is a partial exception: he
can
write dramatic songs, as the Broadway success of “Movin’ Out” showed, and that overt theatricality is one reason that he so often seems cringe or corny to the illuminati.)
Lin-Manuel Miranda grew from a richer mulch: Sondheim worship mixed with a desire to modernize the musical and an ear open to everything. In “
Lin-Manuel Miranda: The Education of an Artist
” (Simon & Schuster), Daniel Pollack-Pelzner traces the formation of someone who was, like many artists, a liminal figure. The son of a Puerto Rican political strategist, Miranda grew up in northern Manhattan but also played as a child at Gracie Mansion. He was indeed the man who would make hip-hop part of the Rodgers tradition, but he did it first at Wesleyan. The beautiful encirclements of American music encircled him, too: Sondheim became his mentor, after Miranda was hired to translate some of the lyrics of “West Side Story” into Spanish for the 2009 revival, giving its Puerto Rican characters more of their own language. Yet his admiration left room for playful off-rhymes. (“I’m afraid it’s unlawful, sir. . . . She’s married to a British officer.”) Like Irving Berlin, Miranda is an instinctive musician whose mistakes can be worth more than other people’s rules. He finds harmonic surprises partly because he doesn’t know he shouldn’t. One realizes, by the biography’s end, that Miranda is doing with hip-hop what his predecessors did with jazz and the blues, and that, as a Puerto Rican, he occupies a place between white and Black, as did his Jewish predecessors on Broadway. His template for “In the Heights” was a favorite show of his, “Fiddler on the Roof.”
That breadth of influence helps explain why “Hamilton” is no more a hip-hop musical than “Porgy and Bess” is a blues musical. Its palette is broad, moving from comic to straight rap, from Cab Calloway swing to Beyoncé-style ballads, each idiom chosen for its dramatic purpose. “Hamilton” fulfills the musical’s original cultural function with extraordinary amplitude: turning the music of streets and dance floors into storytelling, and making American music whole.
One thing becomes clear in all these books: Broadway’s dominant disposition has long been liberal in a capacious sense, hospitable to difference and drawn to the possibilities of a shared American life. It goes without saying that first-class music and art can cut in every ideological direction, and American folk and country music are often deeply conservative—reacting to social alteration with alarm, as working-class Americans often do. Merle Haggard and even Bob Dylan find their essential subject in modernity’s threat to a coherent American mythology. But every long-remembered Broadway musical has had a liberal politics and a liberal breadth beneath it. And truly liberal rather than leftist: pluralistic, optimistic, committed to the ideal of integration that Broadway’s music exemplifies more fully than almost any other American art form, as different traditions find ways to live together within a shared musical language.
We don’t think of “My Fair Lady” as political in the way “West Side Story” is, but its cosmopolitan, outward-looking sensibility belongs squarely to Adlai Stevenson liberalism. “Guys and Dolls,” seemingly apolitical, becomes, in the hands of its book writer Abe Burrows, a hymn to the coexistence of New York’s Irish, Italian, and Jewish worlds, with room even for the Salvation Army. The delight of Nicely-Nicely Johnson’s revival-meeting song lies in how readily a Jewish gambler takes up the language of evangelical Christianity. “The Music Man,” far from being nostalgic Americana, is anti-Iowa: the con man Harold Hill is a gift to the straitened, parched culture of River City, Iowa, and its librarians. And “West Side Story” ends with Jets and Sharks solemnly, if improbably, united in carrying Tony’s body away.
Perhaps the crisis of the musical reflects the crisis of liberal America. A theatre that imagines a shared life needs an audience drawn from many kinds of lives. Its economics increasingly work against that ambition. When a manageable investment can bring a decent return, producers can risk something unfamiliar, and audiences can afford to try it. As the stakes rise on both sides of the footlights, familiarity becomes insurance.
The great eras of popular dramatic art have generally depended on broad access. Shakespeare’s Globe charged a penny for standing room and sixpence for its best seats: tiered prices brought different classes into the same house. Broadway once worked more recognizably on that principle. When “A Chorus Line” opened there, in 1975, its top ticket cost fifteen dollars, or around ninety today. A persuasive case can be made that the economics of the Broadway musical in 1960 resembled those of Shakespeare’s Globe more closely than those of Broadway today, with its extremes of expense. Affordability helped make theatre a habit, and the habit sustained the risks that made theatre an art.
That regular audience is theatre’s condition of existence. Great art can emerge from a garden cottage in Massachusetts or a madhouse in the South of France and find its audience generations later. Theatre needs its audience tonight. Even the highest tragedies, from “King Lear” to “Death of a Salesman,” must first of all offer their customers the prospect of a nice night out. Even as common rituals dwindle, the shared passion persists: people still want that night out. The show must go on because someone wants to see it. Eleven o’clock now happens at nine-thirty. Still, it happens. ♦

epub_24.text:
By
Rebecca Mead
In the past eighteen months, Britain’s venerable Victoria & Albert Museum has added two new outposts. The nation’s most important repository of applied and decorative arts, it possesses far more than its custodians can (or would want to) put on permanent display at its long-standing location, in South Kensington. For decades, hundreds of thousands of its objects were available only to scholars and curators. The museum finally decided to find a way to both store and display its excess holdings, and the inspired result, the Storehouse, opened in East London in May, 2025. Designed by the architectural studio of Diller Scofidio + Renfro, it is a coolly contemporary solution to the puzzle of an inordinate collection: warehouse meets
Wunderkammer
. Then, this past April, another building, the V. & A. East, opened, with an inviting anthropological focus: Why are humans so driven to make things? In our age of A.I. slop, the V. & A.’s devotion to physical objects is a tonic. And if two new buildings seem like overkill, think of all those data centers.
The Storehouse is gargantuan, extending over four airy, interconnected levels and containing a quarter of a million objects. Visitors explore vast corridors of metal racks filled with bentwood chairs, bicycles, and beyond. Objects on display range from the very small—a Palladian-style, mahogany doll’s house from the seventeen-twenties—to the very large. A darkened galley is dedicated to examples from the museum’s collection of stage cloths; it currently hosts a design by Natalia Goncharova for a 1926 Ballets Russes production of “The Firebird.” Measuring more than thirty feet by fifty feet, the cloth invites a jeté from more agile museumgoers. Visiting the Storehouse is like browsing an
IKEA
filled with irreplaceable items. Instead of Sektion kitchen cabinets, there’s the Frankfurt Kitchen, a model of modernist efficiency designed, in the nineteen-twenties, by the architect Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky and retrieved from an apartment in Frankfurt. Instead of Billy bookcases, there’s a gorgeous office—a symphony of cypress surfaces—that Frank Lloyd Wright created for a department-store mogul.
Visitors can’t touch the Wright office—there are limits to accessibility—but they can reserve delicate items from the archive in advance and examine them in a study area. A fashion enthusiast, say, can summon a Balenciaga dress from 1954 or an eighteenth-century mantua gown with a skirt as wide as an automobile. The building’s size has accommodated the installation of large-scale architectural holdings, including a three-story section of the concrete façade of Robin Hood Gardens, an influential brutalist public-housing project in East London. (Completed in 1972, it was recently demolished.) Visitors can walk along a reconstruction of what the building’s architects, Alison and Peter Smithson, characterized as a “street in the sky”—a covered walkway. An accompanying recording of residents’ voices attests to the sense of community that the design fostered.
The V. & A. East, playfully designed by the Irish firm O’Donnell + Tuomey, resembles a billowing concrete skirt. Its programming draws from the surrounding borough of Newham, which is one of London’s most vibrant and diverse districts, with more than a hundred different languages spoken among its residents. A visitor entering the two permanent Why We Make galleries is immersed in a buzzy sense of generative energy and self-expression. One eye-catching display is dedicated to the work of Ron Hitchins, a self-taught artist from East London who, in the late twentieth century, adorned his home with tiles carved in abstract relief patterns of his own devising. Nearby is a ballet costume, from 1987, inspired by the night-club garb of the performance artist Leigh Bowery. The ensemble includes a fabric mask covered in elaborate appliqué crewelwork and a codpiece bedazzled with pink sequins. This kind of cross-pollination—bondage wear combined with eighteenth-century pastoral—will surely inspire students at the neighboring London College of Fashion.
Visitors move from one thrilling juxtaposition to the next. A patchwork quilt made by inmates at Wandsworth Prison, in southwest London, features an embroidered fingerprint flanked by strands of coiled DNA and the words “I didn’t do it Guv!! Honest!” A sampler embroidered around 1830 by Elizabeth Parker, a seventeen-year-old servant, takes the convention’s form—to demonstrate the fineness of a practitioner’s needlework—and turns it into a gripping narrative of abuse by her employer. In neat red stitches, Parker explains that “for trying to avoid the wicked design of my master I was thrown down stairs.” Nearby is a talismanic shirt inscribed with the entire text of the Quran. The shirt, likely made in India around five hundred years ago, was intended to protect its wearer in battle—or in childbirth. I didn’t expect a museum of craft and design to move me so, but I found myself on the brink of tears, struck by the palpable humanity of those who had made, and worn, such works. The armpits of the Quran shirt are stained with centuries-old sweat.
The V. & A., founded in 1852, has tears aplenty in its history. Much of its collection is a product of imperial extraction. In the eighteen-eighties, it absorbed twenty thousand objects from the former India Museum, which was founded by the East India Company. This notorious commercial entity, a precursor of the global corporations of today and big enough to command its own army, ruthlessly exploited foreign resources, human and material. One of the most celebrated objects from the India Museum is a mechanical wooden sculpture of a ferocious tiger gnawing at a British soldier’s throat. It was stolen from the palace of Tipu Sultan, the ruler of Mysore, after he was killed in an assault by British forces in 1799.
Reckoning with the bloody history of global conquest has become a task for all museums whose collections are legacies of colonial control. But Tristram Hunt, the V. & A.’s director, has noted that it is “impossible and ahistorical to seek to ‘decolonise’ a museum like the V. & A., given its foundational connection to the history of British imperialism.” Instead, Hunt has argued, the V. & A. museums explicitly seek to represent a version of British culture that incorporates the historical fact of empire—rather than simply repudiating it, as some on the left might wish, or celebrating it, as some on the right might do. One years-long project is attempting to recover where, and by whom, the India Museum’s objects were made, thus conjuring “the world they inhabited before they were obscured by empire,” as Hunt has written.
After all, this history is constitutive of current British culture. Among the U.K. residents who visit these museums, there will be some who go see relatives in Mysore every year; others will be descendants of people employed by the East India Company. It has become commonplace to speak of multicultural societies like Britain, and cities like London, as being mosaics in which many fragments cohere into a gorgeous whole, or tapestries woven of varied threads. These metaphors take on fresh force at a museum whose collection contains so many mosaics and so many textiles, and which is increasingly dedicated to uncovering the personal stories of their makers.
This is especially true when the skilled fashionings of the human hand—not to mention the cogitations of the human mind—are being displaced by digital simulacra. One of the Why We Make galleries features a remarkable work called “Anatomy of an AI System,” by Kate Crawford and Vladan Joler. Created in 2018, it maps myriad manufacturing processes underlying the Amazon Echo, from the mining of rare-earth metals to the pollutant-producing manufacture of components and the laying of submarine cable. A handy sidebar shows the monthly remuneration of people involved in the Echo’s making, from a C.E.O. towering at the top to a Congolese miner at the bottom. The entire piece is, appropriately enough, too big to take in in one glance; a viewer must step from side to side, and peer and squint, to make any sense of it. The sun has long since set on the British Empire, but, as this work reminds us, it has not set on practices of rapacious exploitation. The rest of the museum’s collection underscores the precious value of taking matters, and materials, into our own hands. ♦

epub_25.text:
The Theatre
Political Skirmishes in “Other Desert Cities” and “A Bright Room Called Day”
Revivals of plays by Jon Robin Baitz and Tony Kushner.
By
Emily Nussbaum
The “Desert” cast is off-kilter, like billiard balls only sometimes landing in the pocket.Illustration by Chris W. Kim
On the night that I attended the current Broadway revival of Jon Robin Baitz’s 2010 play, “Other Desert Cities,” there was a mad clapper at large, a mercenary determined to let us know whose side he was on. It was clear which actor he favored: Joe Keery, who shot to fame on the Netflix hit “Stranger Things” as the moody, mulleted Steve Harrington, a small-town doofus drafted into a teen militia. In “Other Desert Cities,” Keery plays a different sort of conscript, the quietly perceptive reality-TV producer Trip Wyeth, a louche charmer negotiating a ceasefire between his neocon parents and his sister, Brooke, who is threatening to spill the family’s secrets in the pages of this very magazine. I have no idea whether the clapper was a Keery superfan or just agreed with Trip’s critique of his family, but he wasn’t wrong on either count, with the actor delivering a career-making performance: loose, bright, and unpredictable. After his best speech—a witty stem-winder that ends with the declaration “I am California! And California is not happy!”—I was tempted to clap, too.
Unfortunately, the starry ensemble surrounding Keery felt unevenly weighted and off-kilter, like billiard balls only occasionally landing in the pocket. Baitz’s story is set in Palm Springs, in December, 2004, at the home of Polly and Lyman Wyeth, an opulent sandstone aerie with meditative views of the desert, a massive Christmas tree, and portraits of eminences like Barry Goldwater. The Wyeths are Republican grandees and L.A. royalty: Polly (Julia Louis-Dreyfus, all sparkle and venom) is a retired screenwriter, Lyman (a craggy, mournful Ed Harris) a former Hollywood cowboy. Polly, a verbal sharpshooter in a family of clay pigeons, is a dab hand at witticisms like “Sarcasm is the purview of teen-agers and homosexuals,” but if she’s a casual bigot she’s also a reinventor, a steerer of fates: a Jewish go-getter from Texas, she co-wrote frothy commercial films with her sister, then married into Wasp aristocracy with Lyman, who became a government ambassador after their pal “Ronnie” got elected President. By the time we meet the couple, however, that’s ancient history: the Iraq War is raging, and they rarely leave Palm Springs, where they’re in a right-wing bubble, barely tolerating Polly’s now estranged sister, Silda, a lefty dipsomaniac fresh out of rehab, who is played with leggy relish by Allison Janney. The plot revolves, as it inevitably does in shows like this, around a collective trauma. Here, it’s the loss of a third sibling, a radical son who, in the chaos of the seventies, blew up his life and warped the family trajectory. That’s the dark story Brooke is ready to tell the world in a manuscript she’s brought from Sag Harbor—the world’s least welcome Christmas present.
This material should feel resonant, given how many families are split right now—over
MAGA
, over Israel—and how much of a default confessionalism has become online. (These days, Brooke could post an incendiary tweet storm and skip the airfare.) The script is full of pungent, funny debates about power, with observations that still land. “Families get terrorized by their weakest member,” Polly argues. And Trip tells Brooke, “Isn’t it revenge enough that everyone worries about you all the time?” If the exposition creaks, the cast is sprightly, and, for a long time, it’s a blast to watch them spar, particularly Louis-Dreyfus, who scores laughs off the smallest phrases—a disgusted “amongst the Basques,” say. Together, she and Harris capture something formidable about the slice of Old Hollywood the Wyeths represent—sybaritic and hypocritical, brined in self-pity but with a fierce, glamorous quality.
The primary problem is, unfortunately, Lily Rabe, who plays Brooke in a different, blunter register than everyone else onstage. I’ve seen Rabe give beautiful, varied performances, from her dignified Hermione in this past summer’s “The Winter’s Tale” to her demon-possessed nun in “American Horror Story,” gyrating saucily to “You Don’t Own Me.” In “Other Desert Cities,” she’s all sulk and grimace. To be fair, it’s a hard role: Brooke is a solipsistic bummer, a frustrated writer who spends months in a mental hospital being tended to by her mother, then ambushes her with a score-settling tell-all. Instead of seeming righteous but flawed, Rabe’s Brooke validates Polly’s harsh judgment that she’s a reckless brat convinced her truth is the only truth. When, in the final act, a twist reframes the Wyeths’ behavior as, if not fully sympathetic, more understandable, it just made me furrow my brow. By then, it was hard to imagine Brooke’s parents opening up and easier to imagine them manipulating her—defusing, by any means necessary, their daughter’s incendiary literary device.
Even so, I had fun. I loved every costume and considered trying to dress more like a Palm Springs Republican, as Polly would want me to. And there was even, perversely, a touch of escapism to the experience. “Other Desert Cities,” so topical in 2010, now feels as if it were written in the Paleolithic era. If the Wyeths are monsters, they’re also dinosaurs, eclipsed by the nihilists who followed. There’s a wonderful moment when Harris puts on a show, mimicking the death scenes he specialized in onscreen: he buckles at phantom gunshots, then mimes shock, his torso atilt. It was his one true skill, Lyman says, modestly, with a Reaganite twinkle—he always knew how to make an exit.
Two nights later, I went to Crown Heights to catch a revival of a play that felt much more timely, despite having débuted in 1987 and being set in the nineteen-thirties. A tiny, passionate production of Tony Kushner’s “A Bright Room Called Day,” directed by Rachel Gita Karp, was being staged in a town house in the heart of Brooklyn’s so-called Commie Corridor, which helped steer Mayor Zohran Mamdani to victory. As I reclined on a sofa, sipping rosé, a cadre of Berlin bohemians—Reds, fellow- travellers, anarchists, and homosexuals; actors, socialist-realist painters, and writers—began celebrating New Year’s Eve, 1932, at a kitchen table just a few feet away. Lifting glasses of champagne, they toasted, giddily, to “health, happiness, and relative safety on this fierce and splendid night and for many years to come.” It flashed me back to nights of political hope in recent decades, and I felt sick.
“Day” is Kushner’s début—his early problem play, which premièred, in San Francisco, four years before “Angels in America.” At the time, the project felt hyperbolic, largely because of the finger-wagging interventions of Zillah, a modern-day punk anarchist who ranted about Reagan as a new Hitler. (With “Angels,” Kushner found a more fruitful comparison: Roy Cohn and the Red Scare.) Zillah’s speeches have since been reworked, most notably in a 2019 production in which a Kushner-y character called Xillah debated her, framing the story with an anxious meta-narrative. By then, the Hitler comparisons had a different feel: if Kushner had once been the boy who cried wolf, the wolf was at the door.
In 2026, the gemlike Brooklyn venue lent Kushner’s project a magical quality, turning the audience into ghosts from the future, eavesdropping on the fall of the Weimar Republic but unable to intervene. There was no meta frame, and although Zillah still chimed in, it was in smaller doses—and the truth is, we no longer needed her guidance. As the characters playfully debated the rise of Fascism, the dialogue often felt transcribed from some Brooklyn polycule. Is class the best lens for understanding Hitler’s appeal, or is daddy worship? Can anything be learned from sleeping with Nazis? When, ultimately, is it time to flee? The cast was excellent, particularly a sad, sexy Molly Rose Heller as Agnes, a movie actress clinging to her perfect Berlin rental, Jonathan Bock as her Trotskyite beau, a poignant Portal Rose as a sexual adventurer, and Aja Downing as a morally malleable starlet toying with working for the Reich.
Still, the real star was Kushner’s text, a message in a bottle. Witty, bitter, flamboyant, and emotionally grounded, the dialogue swings, delightfully, between intimate exchanges and grandiloquent soliloquies, capturing the vulnerability of idealists in the face of evil. When the Devil himself appeared, in a puff of smoke, the town-house alarm went off and the play paused. For a moment, it all seemed, surreally, to be part of the production: yet another alarm to ignore so that the show could go on. ♦

epub_26.text:
By
Justin Chang
The South Korean writer and director Lee Chang-dong makes beautiful films about terrible things. The question that haunts his stories, giving them a pulsing undertow of dread, is whether those things have already happened or not. In “Secret Sunshine” (2010), a young widow moves to a new town with her son; tragedy has scarred them both, but the film, relentless in its ability to surprise, has even graver ills in store. “Peppermint Candy,” which had its première in 1999, unspools a nightmare in reverse: it opens with a man’s suicide, then rewinds gradually, through two decades of accumulated agonies, to reveal how he got there. In Lee’s movies, time tends to flow inexorably in a single direction, sans flashbacks (or flash-forwards). We see the characters’ histories in their anxious posture, their stricken faces, their frustrated yearning for a glimmer of transcendence.
Time works a bit differently in “Possible Love,” Lee’s first feature since the masterly psychological drama “Burning” (2018). The pain of this story lies squarely in the past, and Lee, who wrote the script with Oh Jung-mi, proves more willing than usual to bridge the gap between then and now. The outset is linear enough. We are in an unnamed town where, two years earlier, a manufacturer named SP Heavy Industries laid off forty per cent of its workforce. The workers organized a strike, but their efforts were brutally suppressed. Among the terminated is a welder, Choi Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), who wears a frown so implacable that it might have been etched in steel. He has since found another manufacturing job, and his sharp-witted, warm-spirited wife, Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon), works at a protective-face-mask factory. They have a young son, Cheol, an ordinary kid with a telltale core of solemnity. The Chois can’t shake their memories of more prosperous times, or of the profit-motivated culling that brought them to an end.
They are not alone in their trauma. We meet the Chois on their way to a memorial gathering for a former colleague of Ho-seok’s who took his own life. The grief of those in attendance goes beyond one death; they seem zombified by their anguish. One woman, though, stands calmly apart. Her name is Lee Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), and she’s shooting a documentary about laid-off workers. Ye-ji is an amateur but she has a muckraker’s instinct for drama. When Mi-ok whisks a cup of soju away from Ho-seok—he’s an alcoholic, and has promised never to drink in public—Yeji, anticipating an outburst, thrusts her lens into the fray. “Do we amuse you?” Ho-seok growls at her. She apologetically lowers her camera, though not for long. She knows there’s a story here, and Lee does, too.
Despite this inauspicious start, Mi-ok and Ye-ji become fast friends. So enlivened are they in each other’s company—and so gracefully does Jeon’s performance harmonize with Cho’s—that you’re tempted to forget Ye-ji’s ulterior motives. But Mi-ok is never blind to them, or to another complicating fact: her new friend is very wealthy. At one point, she calmly calls her out for wearing a pricey-looking shirt while interviewing people who’ve been laid off. Ye-ji has a hunky hedge-fund-type husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), who condescendingly tolerates, but doesn’t finance, his wife’s cinematic caprices. Seeing her attempt to empathize with her subjects, Sang-woo extends the most backhanded of compliments. “You’re different from those people. But you yourself believe that you’re the same,” he says. “That’s great.”
Ye-ji blanches at that jab but only tightens her grip on her project: the Chois are to be the battered working-class foundation of her vérité masterpiece. Ho-seok wants no part of it. Inarticulate with self-loathing, he can scarcely drag himself to his ex-colleagues’ regular group-therapy sessions, let alone unburden himself on camera. But Mi-ok is game to be interviewed, and her words spring to life in wistfully lovely flashbacks. Here she is as a young girl, witnessing, for the first time, the depths of her mother’s working-class shame. And here she is as a teen-ager, catching the eye of a brashly confident Ho-seok, and sensing, with a thrill, that her sheltered world has finally burst open. The first time I saw “Possible Love,” these forays into the past, for all their dewy poignancy, felt like missteps—a rare concession to the backstory gods. Only on a subsequent viewing did I see the craftiness in Lee’s design: Are these Mi-ok’s tearily recalled flashbacks? Or are they being imagined by Ye-ji, eager to transform her subject’s every reverie into a reënactment?
All of which is to say that “Possible Love” is a multitasking marvel: a drama about the fragility of unions, in every sense, wrapped in a seminar on documentary ethics, but one with implications for the fiction realm, too. In an interview, Lee has said that it’s no coincidence he and Ye-ji share a surname, however common. He employs a lightly jostling handheld camera that insidiously mimics the formal syntax of Ye-ji’s documentary—and, in so doing, leaves the mere idea of authorial objectivity by the wayside. (The cinematographer is Kim Ji-yong.) Lee seems to be acknowledging his own potential for dramatic exploitation, if not of his characters, then of the events that inspired the story—an automaker’s restructuring in Korea in 2009 that threatened thousands of layoffs, leading to both a strike and a police crackdown. Lee knows that the liberties of fiction do not absolve him of a responsibility to tell the truth.
No wonder some of the film’s most piercing moments are on the periphery. One woman in a group-counselling session recalls the joyous early days of the strike, with their almost sacred spirit of community: “In all my life, I’ve never felt such happiness.” Another speaks of dreading the elevator in her building, lest she run into neighbors who still work at SP Heavy. Lee’s films have often zeroed in on misfits and outcasts, cut off from society’s embrace. What he evokes here is a different kind of alienation, suffused with bitterness and loss: a mass- casualty event that once brought people together must now be suffered in isolation. The boldest declarations of solidarity, Lee knows, often precede the quietest and cruellest of betrayals.
After the film’s première, at the Venice International Film Festival (where it won the Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize), more than a few observers invoked another class-conscious, double-decker marriage story from Korea: Bong Joon Ho’s “Parasite” (2019). (In both films, Cho Yeo-jeong, evidently cursed with resting rich face, plays the wealthier of two wives.) Lee’s contemplative realism could hardly be further removed from Bong’s blood-slicked flamboyance, but let’s indulge the reductive comparison. Like “Parasite,” “Possible Love” leads us into an enviable piece of real estate—Sang-woo’s family vacation home, a beachside paradise that was built for knotty third acts. But Lee, who has been known to gut his characters in the final stretch, doesn’t raise the body count to Bongian proportions. There is violence here, but it comes at us obliquely, with no inflection or exaggeration—in a sex scene that shivers with menace, or through a grimly mediated screen of documentary footage. Physical force has a hundred ways to shock and linger, but, crucially, it isn’t granted the last word.
The title asks whether love can survive what life throws at it: unemployment, depression, addiction, disappointment, poverty. A superficial glance would conclude that Ye-ji and Sang-woo are a dream couple, yet the more we see of them, the more glaring their lack of emotional capital. Miraculously, though, whenever the camera shifts to Ho-seok and Mi-ok—whether they’re bickering on their way home or scarfing down late-night snacks on the kitchen floor—love feels not just possible but plausible. Sul and Jeon have admittedly had plenty of practice; this is the third movie, after “I Wish I Had a Wife” and “Birthday,” in which they’ve played a couple. Both actors have also worked with Lee before, to tremendous effect. Sul was the suicidal protagonist of “Peppermint Candy,” and Jeon was the grieving heroine of “Secret Sunshine”—two performances that, for sustained emotional force, have few rivals in the acting annals of this century. They, too, are part of the past that haunts “Possible Love.”
Faced with such a high-stakes reunion, the actors, wisely, rise to the challenge with exacting understatement. You keep waiting for Sul to explode, but Ho-seok’s sadness lies beyond histrionics, and we realize that he isn’t angry or distant by nature; his decency cost him almost everything, and he now wields detachment as a shield against further harm. Without his wife to chide and console him, where would he be? Mi-ok feels her family’s losses acutely, but her impishly defiant spirit—watch as she tells her boss she’s starting a union, almost on a whim, like a goofball Norma Rae—has armored her against despair. And Jeon, in the most intricately detailed and emotionally liberated performance I’ve seen this year, gives flesh and definition to the character’s sardonic sense of mischief, her sudden spasms of grief, and her deep understanding that the most romantic gestures can be the most pragmatic. Hence the gorgeous moment when Mi-ok joins Ho-seok for a nightcap under the stars—secret moonshine—and affirms that, in the face of insurmountable problems, enduring them together is their only solution. “Drinking without you, it’s so bitter,” Ho-seok says. Solidarity forever. ♦

By
Alfred Corn
Faces and names warm waves kept washing in,
Decades of faces that recur, no matter
If names don’t surface, drowned out now, unlike
Their words and voiceprints—counsel, banter, twists
Of phrasing still heard even if the speakers
Have slipped away in some rough undertow,
Departures now confirmed or probable,
Given how many rising tides have fallen.
The psyche: a kind of twine, a cordage spun
Of optic fibre drawn from a thousand minds—
Strands this instant wondering if yarns
Of mine in turn wound up in others’ cable,
A hawser mooring then to now and selves
Whose face and words remain, if not their names.

By
Adrienne Raphel
I’m in Miami, sign here. I return to collect my former self
And every day I leave with a new one.
I have bought one a day for the past forty-eight days.
My, do I wear many hats!
Floppy for photo ops,
Baseball for redundancy,
Plinth for protection,
Rattan plinth for recipes,
Gingham for controversy.
And every morning Bob’s Barricades rebuild,
It isn’t hard when there’s nothing behind it.
My photo op. I need to need this.
Miami is shaped like a design
Of anything I need.
If I stuff the pain down with more pain
There will be more numbers
One two three four five six.
When I lost access to my password,
I regained it only through months
Of physical therapy muscle memory.
I write it the wrong way
So when I, too, lose access to my left side
And they try to put it together
No one will know this piece of me.
My followers will raise so much in honor of my hats,
That short-lived but most lucrative period of my life,
I never know what’s going to bring me fame, but I’m lucky if I get it
Even if only for forty-eight hours of frost.
